quiz.why: Written, agreed expectations reduce surprises in reviews.

lessons.title: When you mess up: owning and recovering

scenes.text: Sam Fernandes, three weeks into a Goa-based fintech, runs a clean-up script on what he thinks is his local database. It is the shared staging database. The QA team's test data disappears.
His first instinct is to hide it and hope someone else gets blamed. His hands are shaking.
Instead, within ten minutes he messages his lead: 'I made a mistake — I ran the clean-up script against staging. QA test data is gone. I've stopped the script. How can I help restore it?'
The lead restores a backup in an hour. In the review, the team adds a confirmation prompt to the script. Sam's honesty is mentioned positively in his first feedback.

steps.title: Mistakes are expected; hiding them is not
steps.body:
Every professional makes mistakes. Managers mostly judge you on **what happens next**. A simple recovery formula:
- **1. Stop the bleeding** — if something is still breaking, stop it (stop the script, pause the email campaign).
- **2. Tell the right person quickly** — usually your lead or manager, within minutes for anything affecting others.
- **3. State facts, not excuses** — what happened, impact, what you've done so far.
- **4. Offer help with the fix.**
- **5. Learn and prevent** — suggest a process fix (a checklist, a confirmation prompt, a review step).

steps.title: Worked example: a good 'I made a mistake' message
steps.body:
*'Hi Rakesh — I made an error. I sent the draft invoice to the client instead of the final one at 3:10 pm. The difference is the tax line (₹18,400). I haven't contacted the client yet. Could you advise whether you or I should send a correction? I've prepared the correct version and a short note.'*

It has: what happened, when, the impact, what has not yet been done, a question about next steps, and a prepared solution.

steps.title: Blameless reviews (RCAs)
steps.body:
Many tech companies do **blameless post-mortems** or **RCAs (root cause analyses)** after incidents. The idea: people rarely fail on purpose; systems allow mistakes. A good RCA asks *'Why was it possible to run that script on staging?'* rather than *'Who is the idiot?'*

A common technique is the **5 Whys**: keep asking 'why' until you reach a process cause you can fix. As a fresher, contributing honestly to an RCA is a chance to show maturity.

steps.title: What makes it worse
steps.body:
- Hiding or deleting evidence (logs, emails).
- Blaming tools, teammates or 'unclear instructions' as your first sentence.
- Over-apologising for days — one sincere apology plus action is enough.
- Repeating the same mistake: that is when trust really drops. Write down your lesson.

steps.title: Look after yourself too
steps.body: The first big mistake can feel crushing, especially if you are the first in your family in a corporate job and carry everyone's expectations. Talk to a trusted senior or friend, sleep, and remember: one mistake handled well usually *increases* trust. If you feel persistently anxious or low, talk to someone — your company may offer a confidential Employee Assistance Programme (EAP), and India's Tele-MANAS helpline is 14416.

a.text: You realise you emailed a client the wrong pricing file 20 minutes ago. Your manager is in a meeting. What do you do first?

choices.label: Message your manager immediately with the facts and ask how to correct it
choices.feedback: Fast, factual escalation is exactly right.

choices.label: Wait and hope the client doesn't open it
choices.feedback: Hoping rarely works; the client may act on wrong prices.

choices.label: Email the client yourself saying 'please ignore' without telling anyone
choices.feedback: Well-meant, but the client relationship belongs to your manager; uncoordinated messages can confuse.

b.text: Your manager replies: 'Thanks for flagging. Send a short correction from your account, cc me.' What do you write?

choices.label: A brief note: 'Please disregard the earlier file; the correct version is attached. Apologies for the confusion.'
choices.feedback: Short, clear and professional.

choices.label: A long emotional apology explaining your whole week
choices.feedback: Too much. Clients want clarity, not drama.

c.text: Next morning the client calls your manager asking why prices went up 15%. Your manager asks you if you know anything.

choices.label: Admit it honestly now and offer to help fix it
choices.feedback: Late, but honesty now still limits damage.

choices.label: Say you have no idea
choices.feedback: Lying turns a small mistake into a trust problem.

d.text: The client replies to everyone asking which prices are final; your manager is surprised. What now?

choices.label: Explain to your manager immediately and apologise for not looping them in
choices.feedback: Good recovery — always loop in the owner.

e1.text: Mistake fixed in under an hour. Your manager trusts you more because you flagged it fast.

e2.text: It's fixed, but next time keep corrections short and factual.

e3.text: The damage is contained. Lesson: escalate early and let the relationship owner decide the client message.

e4.text: Email logs show it was you. Now the issue is honesty, not a file — a much harder thing to repair. Always own it.

quiz.q: What is the first step if your mistake is still causing damage?
options: Stop the damage (e.g., stop the script)
quiz.why: Containment comes first; explanations come after.

quiz.q: What is a 'blameless post-mortem'?
options: A review focusing on how the system allowed the mistake, to prevent repeats
A review that ignores the problem
A meeting to decide who gets fired
quiz.why: Blameless reviews look for process fixes and encourage honest reporting.

quiz.q: Which opening line is best when reporting your mistake?
options: 'I made an error: here is what happened and the impact…'
quiz.why: Owning it and stating facts builds trust.

quiz.q: The '5 Whys' technique is used to…
options: Find a root cause by repeatedly asking why
quiz.why: Asking 'why' repeatedly moves from the symptom to a fixable process cause.

questions.q: Onboarding is best treated as…
options: Your first project that you actively drive
questions.why: Driving your own onboarding gets you productive faster.

questions.q: Which is a good first-1:1 question?
options: Who is the laziest person here?
What does success look like for me in 30 and 90 days?

questions.q: A 'first-week notebook' should include…
questions.why: These four headings become your personal team wiki.

questions.q: Before starting a task, you should confirm…
options: Who else got a similar task
What, why, when and how good
questions.why: These four questions prevent most misunderstandings.

questions.q: 'Playing back' a task means…
options: Repeating your understanding in writing so the requester can correct it
Asking someone else to do it
questions.why: A written playback catches misunderstandings early.

questions.q: Who typically owns release sign-off in a software team?
options: The QA lead or release owner
questions.why: Quality/release owners decide whether work ships.

questions.q: Gold-plating means…
options: Polishing work far beyond what was needed
questions.why: Over-polishing wastes time when 'rough' was requested.

questions.q: You reported 'on track' daily, then 'delayed' on the deadline day. The core problem is…
options: Late bad news — risks should be flagged early
questions.why: Early warnings let managers re-plan; surprises damage trust.

questions.q: Which is the BEST mistake-reporting message?
options: 'I sent the draft invoice instead of the final at 3:10 pm; the tax line differs by ₹18,400; I have the correct version ready — should you or I send the correction?'
questions.why: It states facts, impact, status and a prepared fix.

questions.q: Why does a 30-60-90 plan protect you at appraisal time?
options: It records agreed expectations you can show you met
questions.why: Agreed written goals make your review fairer and evidence-based.

questions.q: In an RCA, the best question after 'the script deleted staging data' is…
options: Why was it possible to run it on staging without a safeguard?
questions.why: Blameless RCAs target fixable system causes.

questions.q: Your manager is unavailable, and your mistake affects a client right now. The best approach is usually…
options: Contact the manager or their designated backup quickly with facts and let the relationship owner decide the client message
questions.why: Escalate fast through the right channel; coordinate client communication.

questions.q: Which combination builds trust fastest in the first 90 days?
options: Early drafts, clear updates, early risk flags and honest ownership of mistakes
questions.why: Visible reliability and honesty matter more than heroics.

courses.title: Emails, meetings and Teams/Slack etiquette
courses.summary: How to write emails people read, behave well in meetings, use chat tools without annoying anyone, and ask for help the smart way.
outcomes: Learners can write clear professional emails with good subject lines and asks
Learners can prepare for, contribute to and document meetings
Learners can use Teams/Slack with good etiquette across time zones
Learners can ask for help in a way that gets quick, good answers

scenes.text: Divya, a fresher in a Chennai bank's operations team, emails five people with the subject 'Query'. The email is three paragraphs long and the actual question is in the last line.
Two days pass. No reply. She feels ignored.
Her senior, Lakshmi, rewrites it: subject 'Action needed by Thu: approval for KYC exception (Account 4471)', the ask in the first line, one person in 'To', others in 'Cc'.
Reply in 40 minutes. Divya learns that busy people scan emails in seconds — the structure does the work.

steps.title: Subject line = the headline
steps.body:
A good subject line tells the reader **what it is about and what you need**, so they can prioritise without opening it.
- Weak: *'Query'*, *'Hi'*, *'Urgent!!!'*
- Strong: *'Approval needed by Thu: KYC exception for account 4471'*
- Strong: *'FYI: Release 2.3 moved to 14 March'*
- Strong: *'Decision needed: vendor A vs B for printing (2-min read)'*

Prefixes like **Action needed**, **FYI**, **Decision needed** are widely understood.

steps.title: Bottom line up front (BLUF)
steps.body:
Put your **ask or conclusion in the first one or two lines**, then context. Structure:
- **Line 1:** what you need and by when.
- **Context:** 2–4 short lines or bullets.
- **Details/attachments:** for those who want them.
- **Close:** a clear next step.

Use short paragraphs and bullets. If an email needs scrolling on a phone, consider a call or a document instead.

steps.title: Worked example: before and after
steps.body:
**Before:** *'Dear Sir, Greetings of the day. Hope you are doing well. As discussed I was checking the account and there seems to be some issue with the KYC because the documents are old and the customer says… Kindly do the needful.'*

**After:** *'Hi Rajesh, Could you approve a 15-day KYC exception for account 4471 by Thursday? Context: the customer's address proof expired last month; renewed proof is submitted to the passport office (receipt attached). Without approval, the account freezes on Friday. Thanks, Divya'*

The second version is shorter, clearer and answerable in one click.

steps.title: To, Cc, Bcc and Reply-all
steps.body:
- **To:** people who must act or reply.
- **Cc:** people who need to know but not act. Don't Cc a manager just to 'pressure' someone — it is usually noticed.
- **Bcc:** rarely; e.g., large external lists to protect addresses. Avoid secretly Bcc'ing people on sensitive discussions.
- **Reply-all:** only when everyone on the thread needs your reply. 'Thanks!' to 200 people is not needed.
- Before sending: check attachments, names, tone, and that client data goes only to authorised people.

steps.title: Phrases to retire
steps.body:
Some phrases common in Indian offices can confuse global readers or sound dated:
- *'Kindly do the needful'* → say exactly what you need.
- *'Please revert'* → *'Please reply'* (globally, 'revert' means 'go back to a previous state').
- *'PFA'* → *'Attached is…'*
- *'Greetings of the day'* → a simple *'Hi Rajesh,'* is fine in most modern workplaces.

None of these are 'wrong', but clarity wins, especially with international colleagues.

activity.prompt: Sort each subject line: does it help the reader prioritise?

items.text: Action needed by Fri: sign-off on Q3 test plan
Query
FYI: Office closed on 2 Oct (Gandhi Jayanti)
URGENT!!!!
Decision needed: choose venue A or B for offsite
Hi
Re: Re: Re: Fwd: update

quiz.q: What does BLUF mean in an email?
options: Bottom Line Up Front — the ask or conclusion first
quiz.why: Leading with the ask helps busy readers act quickly.

quiz.q: Who belongs in the 'To' field?
options: People who must act or reply
quiz.why: 'To' signals responsibility to act; 'Cc' is for information.

quiz.q: For global colleagues, 'please revert' is better written as…
quiz.why: Outside South Asia 'revert' usually means 'go back', so 'reply' is clearer.

quiz.q: When should you avoid email and switch to a call or document?
options: When the email needs lots of scrolling or back-and-forth
quiz.why: Complex or emotional topics are often better handled live or in a structured doc.

scenes.text: Imran joins a daily stand-up with a London client team. He keeps his camera off, mumbles 'same as yesterday', and leaves.
In a month, the client lead asks Imran's manager, 'What exactly is Imran working on?'
His manager coaches him: prepare three lines before every stand-up, speak first sometimes, and send short notes after important calls.
Six weeks later, the client lead praises 'Imran's crisp updates'. Same work — better meeting habits.

steps.title: Before: prepare in five minutes
steps.body:
- Read the agenda and any pre-read. If there is no agenda, it is fine to ask the organiser politely: *'Is there anything I should prepare?'*
- Write your **update in three lines**: done, doing next, blockers.
- Note **one question or point** you want to raise.
- Join 1–2 minutes early, test audio, and close noisy tabs and notifications.

steps.title: Worked example: a crisp stand-up update
steps.body:
*'Yesterday I finished the payment-retry API and raised the PR. Today I'm writing tests and fixing two review comments. One blocker: I need test card numbers from the payments team — Sana, could you point me to the right person after the call?'*

About 20 seconds. Specific. A clear blocker with a named ask. Compare with *'Working on the API, same as yesterday.'*

steps.title: During: contribute even as a junior
steps.body:
- Speak at least once in meetings where your work is discussed — a question counts.
- Use the raise-hand feature or chat if it's hard to get a word in.
- Keep camera on when the team norm is camera-on, especially for client calls and 1:1s (unless bandwidth or privacy prevents it — just say so).
- Don't multitask visibly; people can hear typing.
- If you don't understand something, ask: *'Sorry, could you clarify what UAT sign-off involves here?'* — usually someone else had the same question.

steps.title: After: minutes of meeting (MoM)
steps.body:
For important meetings, someone should send **minutes** within a few hours: decisions, action items (owner + date), and open questions. Freshers who volunteer to take notes become visible and learn fast.

Template:
- **Decisions:** Go-live moved to 14 March.
- **Actions:** Imran — share test report by Wed; Sana — confirm test cards by Tue.
- **Open:** Need client approval on new error messages.

steps.title: Time zones and meeting manners
steps.body: With US/UK/Australia teams, meetings often land early morning or late evening in India. Agree working-hour overlaps, use calendar time-zone features, and say early if a slot clashes with something important. Decline politely with a reason when you truly cannot add value — *'I don't think I'm needed for this one; could you share the notes?'*

activity.prompt: Complete the stand-up formula and the minutes template.
activity.text: A good stand-up covers what I ___, what I'm doing next, and any ___. Minutes list decisions, action items with an ___ and a date, and open questions.

quiz.q: A strong stand-up update includes…
options: What you finished, what's next and specific blockers
quiz.why: Short, specific updates with blockers make you visible and get help fast.

quiz.q: Minutes of meeting should contain…
options: Decisions, action items with owners and dates, and open questions
quiz.why: Minutes turn talk into accountable action.

quiz.q: You don't understand a term used in a meeting. Best response?
options: Google it during the meeting while ignoring everyone
quiz.why: Clarifying questions are normal and often help others too.

quiz.q: Why volunteer to take notes as a fresher?
options: It makes you visible and helps you learn the work
quiz.why: Note-takers understand decisions deeply and are noticed.

scenes.text: Pooja, a fresher in Hyderabad, sends 'hi' to her US-based tech lead, Jason, at 7 pm IST. Then she waits for him to reply before asking her question.
Jason sees 'hi' at 9 am Pacific, replies 'hi?', and goes into meetings. Pooja is asleep. A whole day is lost.
Her teammate shows her the 'no hello' habit: greeting plus full question in one message, with context and links.
Next time, Jason answers in one go, from his phone, between meetings.

steps.title: Greeting + question in one message
steps.body:
Don't send just 'hi' and wait. Write the full message at once:

*'Hi Jason — quick question on the login bug (JIRA-482): should the retry limit be 3 or 5? The spec says 3, but the old code uses 5. Not urgent; today or tomorrow is fine.'*

This respects time zones, lets the person answer asynchronously and tells them the urgency.

steps.title: Channels, threads and DMs
steps.body:
- **Use threads** to reply to a specific message, so channels stay readable.
- **Public channel over DM** for project questions — others learn from the answer, and the knowledge isn't lost. DMs are for personal or sensitive topics.
- **@mentions:** mention a person only when you need them; avoid @channel/@everyone unless it truly concerns everyone now.
- **Status:** keep your status accurate (in a meeting, on leave, focusing). Set an out-of-office when you are away.

steps.title: After-hours and tone
steps.body:
- Messages sent late at night can feel like pressure. Many tools let you **schedule send** for the recipient's working hours.
- Text loses tone. 'Ok.' can sound cold; 'Why did you do this?' can sound like an attack. Prefer *'Could you help me understand the reason for this change?'*
- Avoid all-caps, too many exclamation marks, and sarcasm in writing.
- Never criticise colleagues in chat — screenshots travel, and company chats are company records.

steps.title: Emojis and reactions
steps.body: Emoji reactions (👍 ✅ 👀) are a great way to acknowledge without cluttering a thread — e.g., 👀 = 'I'm looking at it', ✅ = 'done'. Follow team norms: some teams are casual, client channels usually more formal. When unsure, mirror how your seniors write.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Rewrite this message: *'hi'*, *'r u there'*, *'need help'*. Make it one complete message with a greeting, the question, the context (a link or ticket number) and the urgency.

statements.s: Sending just 'hi' and waiting for a reply is efficient across time zones.
statements.why: It forces two round-trips; send the full question at once.

statements.s: Project questions are often better in a public team channel than in a DM.
statements.why: Others benefit and knowledge stays searchable.

statements.s: Using @everyone for a small question is good practice.
statements.why: It interrupts many people; use it only for truly urgent, all-hands information.

statements.s: Scheduling a message for the recipient's working hours is considerate.
statements.why: It avoids after-hours pressure.

statements.s: Company chat messages are private and can never be reviewed.
statements.why: Workplace chats are company records and can be reviewed under policy.

quiz.q: What is the 'no hello' habit?
options: Putting the greeting and the full question in one message
quiz.why: It allows asynchronous answers and saves time.

quiz.q: Why use threads?
options: To keep replies attached to the original topic so channels stay readable

quiz.q: A colleague's change broke your code. Best chat message?
options: Say nothing and revert it secretly
'Could you help me understand the reason for this change? It's affecting the login flow.'
Post a screenshot in the team channel mocking it
quiz.why: Neutral, curious wording keeps it professional.

quiz.q: What does a 👀 reaction commonly signal?
quiz.why: Many teams use 👀 as 'seen, looking into it'.

lessons.title: Asking for help the smart way

scenes.text: Nikhil messages a senior: 'My code is not working. Please help.' The senior asks five follow-up questions over an hour.
Aisha, stuck on the same kind of issue, writes: what she's trying to do, the exact error, what she already tried, and a link to the branch.
The senior spots Aisha's problem in two minutes. 'Great question,' he replies.
Aisha's reputation grows as 'someone who thinks before asking'. Asking well is a skill, not a weakness.

steps.title: The 4-part help request
steps.body:
- **Goal:** what you are trying to achieve.
- **Problem:** what's happening instead (exact error message, screenshot, data).
- **Tried:** what you already tried and what you found.
- **Ask:** the specific help you want (a pointer, a 10-minute call, a review).

This shows effort, saves the helper's time, and often you solve the problem yourself while writing it (sometimes called 'rubber-duck debugging').

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: *'Hi Rahul — I'm trying to generate the monthly GST report from the new dashboard (goal). The export fails with 'Error 403: insufficient permissions' (problem). I checked my role — it says Analyst — and tried a different browser (tried). Do I need a different role, or is there a request form? A pointer is enough (ask). Thanks!'*

steps.title: When to ask
steps.body:
A balanced rule: try genuinely for a reasonable time (often 30–60 minutes for a technical block; less if a deadline or client is affected), then ask. Ask sooner if:
- you lack access or information only someone else has,
- the issue blocks others,
- you're unsure about something risky (production systems, money, legal or client data).

Never 'try things' on production systems or customer data to avoid asking.

steps.title: Getting past hesitation
steps.body: Many Indian freshers hesitate to ask seniors because of hierarchy or fear of looking weak. In most good teams, **not asking** is seen as the bigger problem. Respect seniors' time by asking well, closing the loop (*'That worked, thank you!'*) and documenting the answer for the next person. Thanking publicly in the team channel is a nice touch.

activity.prompt: Arrange the parts of a strong help request in a sensible order.
items: Greet and state your goal
Describe the exact problem or error
Explain what you already tried
Make a specific ask
Close the loop and thank them once solved

quiz.q: Which help request is strongest?
options: Goal, exact error, what you tried, and a specific ask
Asking five people the same question privately
quiz.why: Structured requests are fast to answer and show effort.

quiz.q: When should you ask sooner rather than later?
options: When you're blocked by access only someone else has, or it's risky
quiz.why: Access, blocking others and risk all justify asking quickly.

quiz.q: What is 'closing the loop'?
options: Telling the helper it worked and thanking them
quiz.why: It respects the helper and builds goodwill.

quiz.q: Why might writing a clear request solve the problem itself?
options: Explaining step by step often reveals your own mistake
quiz.why: Articulating the problem clarifies thinking — 'rubber-duck debugging'.

questions.q: The best email subject line is…
options: Action needed by Thu: approve KYC exception for account 4471
questions.why: It states topic, action and deadline.

questions.q: 'Cc' is for people who…
options: Need to know but not act

questions.q: In Teams/Slack, the most efficient first message is…
A good stand-up update is about…
questions.why: Brief and specific respects everyone's time.

questions.q: Which is NOT a good use of @everyone?
options: Production outage affecting the whole team
questions.why: Small questions don't justify interrupting everyone.

questions.q: Minutes of meeting should be sent…
options: Within a few hours, with decisions and owned actions

questions.q: 'Kindly do the needful' is problematic mainly because…
options: It doesn't say what you actually need

questions.q: Project questions are often best asked in…
options: A public team channel or thread
questions.why: Shared answers help everyone and stay searchable.

questions.q: A 4-part help request contains…
questions.why: This structure gets fast, accurate help.

questions.q: You must email 300 external partners. To protect their addresses you'd use…
questions.why: Bcc hides addresses in large external mailings.

questions.q: A text message 'Why did you change this?' may be read as…
options: An accusation; reword with curiosity and context
questions.why: Text loses tone; soften with context and curiosity.

questions.q: Which statement about workplace chat is accurate?
options: It's a company record that may be reviewed under policy
It is deleted every night by law
It's private property of the employee
questions.why: Treat workplace chats as official records.

questions.q: You're unsure whether a fix is safe to run on production. Best action?
options: Ask a batch-mate to run it
Ask before acting, explaining risk and your plan
questions.why: Risky actions on production/customer data require asking first.

courses.title: Appraisals, feedback and your first payslip
courses.summary: How performance cycles work, how to write a self-assessment, how to take feedback, and how to read your offer letter, CTC and payslip in India.
outcomes: Learners can explain how a typical appraisal cycle and rating work
Learners can write an evidence-based self-assessment
Learners can receive and act on feedback, including tough feedback
Learners can read CTC, in-hand pay, PF and payslip components

scenes.text: Rahul worked late all year at a Noida IT firm. In April, he receives 'Meets Expectations' and a 6% hike. His friend in the same team gets 'Exceeds' and 12%.
Rahul is furious: 'I worked harder!' His manager explains that his goals were never updated after he moved projects, and he never shared his wins.
Rahul learns the cycle: goals are set, mid-year check-ins happen, managers rate, and ratings are calibrated across teams.
This year he keeps a 'wins log' and updates goals within a week of any project change.

steps.title: The typical cycle
steps.body:
Details differ, but most companies follow something like:
- **Goal setting** (start of year): what you'll deliver and how you'll be measured.
- **Check-ins** (mid-year and/or quarterly): progress, feedback, adjustments.
- **Self-assessment:** you describe your results and evidence.
- **Manager assessment & rating:** e.g., a 3- or 5-point scale.
- **Calibration:** managers compare ratings across teams so standards are consistent; your manager may need to defend your rating with evidence.
- **Outcome:** rating, increment, bonus, sometimes promotion.

Many companies in India run the cycle around April (aligned with the financial year, April–March), but others use January or other cycles.

steps.title: Ratings and distributions
steps.body:
Some companies use a **forced or guided distribution** (for example, only a limited share of people can get the top rating). Others have moved away from it. If your company uses one, a good rating depends partly on how your contribution compares with peers — which is why **visible, documented impact** matters.

Ask HR or your manager: *What is our rating scale? Is there a guided distribution? When is calibration?*

steps.title: What managers actually evaluate
steps.body:
Usually two things:
- **What** you delivered (results against goals: features shipped, tickets resolved, accuracy, client feedback).
- **How** you delivered (collaboration, ownership, learning, values).

Hours worked are rarely a direct metric. Working late on the wrong things doesn't raise your rating; delivering important things reliably does.

steps.title: Keep a wins log
steps.body:
Every Friday, take five minutes to note:
- What I delivered (with numbers: '*reduced report time from 3 hours to 20 minutes*').
- Appreciation received (save the email or message link).
- Things I learned or certifications completed.
- Help I gave others.

At appraisal time you'll have a year of evidence instead of trying to remember.

steps.title: Common fresher mistakes
steps.body:
- Not updating goals after a project change.
- Assuming the manager knows everything you did.
- Discussing ratings angrily in public channels.
- Comparing increments with friends without knowing their goals, band or market adjustments.

activity.prompt: Put a typical appraisal cycle in order.

quiz.q: What is 'calibration' in appraisals?
options: Managers comparing ratings across teams for consistent standards
quiz.why: Calibration aligns ratings, so evidence of impact matters.

quiz.q: What did Rahul do wrong?
options: He didn't update goals after a project change or share his wins
quiz.why: Outdated goals and invisible wins made his impact hard to rate.

quiz.q: Managers usually evaluate…
options: What you delivered and how you delivered it
quiz.why: Results plus behaviours are the common pair.

quiz.q: A good wins-log entry is…
options: 'Automated the weekly report; time cut from 3 hours to 20 minutes'
quiz.why: Specific, measurable impact is persuasive evidence.

scenes.text: Sneha, a support engineer in Kochi, writes her first self-assessment: 'I am hard working, sincere and a team player. I always do my best.'
Her mentor asks, 'What did you actually achieve? How would someone who doesn't know you believe it?'
She rewrites: 'Resolved 410 tickets with 96% customer satisfaction (team average 91%); wrote 12 knowledge articles that cut repeat tickets on password resets by about a third.'
Her manager copies two lines straight into the calibration sheet. Sneha learns that evidence speaks louder than adjectives.

steps.title: Use the STAR or CAR structure
steps.body:
For each major goal, describe one or two achievements with:
- **Context/Situation:** what the problem was.
- **Action:** what *you* did (use 'I' for your part, 'we' for team work — be honest).
- **Result:** measurable outcome — time saved, errors reduced, revenue, customer feedback, quality.

Tie each achievement to a goal or company priority.

steps.title: Worked example: adjectives vs evidence
steps.body:
**Weak:** *'I am a quick learner and very dedicated.'*

**Strong:** *'Goal: support the new billing module. Context: I had no prior SQL experience. Action: completed an internal SQL course in 3 weeks and built 5 validation queries. Result: QA found 40% fewer data defects in the billing release compared with the previous release.'*

The strong version proves 'quick learner' without saying it.

steps.title: Be honest about gaps
steps.body: Include one or two areas to grow, with a plan: *'I'd like to improve my estimation; I'll break tasks into sub-tasks under 1 day and compare estimates with actuals monthly.'* Managers trust self-assessments that are balanced; one that claims perfection is often discounted.

steps.title: Avoid these
steps.body:
- Copy-pasting your job description.
- Claiming team results as only yours.
- Criticising colleagues in the form.
- Writing two pages — be concise: 3–5 strong achievements beat 20 weak ones.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Pick one thing you did this month. Write it in one sentence with Context, Action and Result, including at least one number.

activity.prompt: Sort each line: evidence or adjective?

items.text: Resolved 410 tickets at 96% CSAT
I am very sincere and hard working
Wrote 12 help articles; repeat tickets dropped about a third
I am a team player
Automated invoice checks, saving ~6 hours a week
I always give 100%

quiz.q: What makes a self-assessment persuasive?
options: Specific actions and measurable results linked to goals
quiz.why: Evidence can be used directly in calibration.

quiz.q: In CAR, the 'R' stands for…
Why include a growth area?
quiz.why: Honesty about gaps, with a plan, builds trust.

quiz.q: How should you describe team achievements?
options: Say what the team did and what your part was

scenes.text: In his mid-year review, Arjun's manager in Mumbai says, 'Your reports have too many small errors. Clients notice.'
Arjun's face burns. He wants to argue that the deadlines were impossible.
He takes a breath and asks, 'Could you show me two examples so I understand the pattern?'
He builds a three-point checklist before sending any report. Three months later his manager says the improvement is obvious.

steps.title: Listen first, respond later
steps.body:
When you get critical feedback:
- **Pause.** Breathe. You don't have to respond immediately.
- **Thank** them — giving feedback is uncomfortable too.
- **Clarify** with examples: *'Could you share a specific instance?'*
- **Summarise:** *'So the issue is small errors in client reports, especially numbers and names.'*
- **Agree a next step** and follow up later. You can disagree, but do it calmly, with facts, after you've understood.

steps.title: Turning feedback into action
steps.body:
Arjun's checklist before sending any report:
- Numbers totalled and cross-checked with source.
- Client name, dates and currency verified.
- Read once aloud (or use read-aloud) for typos.

He then told his manager: *'I've started using this checklist; could you tell me in a month if you see a difference?'* Asking for follow-up feedback shows you took it seriously.

steps.title: Ask for feedback before appraisal time
steps.body:
Don't wait for the annual review. Ask small, specific questions regularly:
- *'What's one thing I could have done better in that client call?'*
- *'On a scale of 1–10, how ready is this document? What would make it a 9?'*

Specific questions get useful answers; 'Any feedback?' usually gets 'All good'.

steps.title: Feedback vs mistreatment
steps.body: Feedback is about your work and behaviour, given respectfully. Insults, public humiliation, comments about your caste, religion, gender, region, body or family, or threats are **not feedback**. Note dates and details and seek help from HR or another trusted senior; harassment of a sexual nature can be raised under the company's POSH policy.

a.text: Your manager says in your 1:1: 'Your presentation yesterday was hard to follow.' You feel defensive. What do you say?

choices.label: 'Thanks for telling me. Which part was hardest to follow?'
choices.feedback: Curiosity turns criticism into useful detail.

choices.label: 'Everyone else's slides were worse.'
choices.feedback: Comparison sounds defensive and ends the learning.

choices.label: Say nothing and look upset
choices.feedback: Your manager can't help if you shut down.

b.text: Manager: 'You started with methodology; the client wanted the recommendation first.' What next?

choices.label: Summarise and propose: 'Next time I'll lead with the recommendation. Could you review my next draft?'
choices.feedback: Clear action plus follow-up request.

choices.label: Argue that methodology is important
choices.feedback: It may be, but first agree on what the audience needs.

c.text: The conversation becomes awkward. Your manager says, 'Let's move on.' What can you still do?

choices.label: Later, message: 'I reacted defensively earlier — could you share more about the presentation?'
choices.feedback: Repairing quickly shows maturity.

choices.label: Avoid the topic forever
choices.feedback: The issue will likely appear in your appraisal.

e1.text: You turned feedback into a plan. Managers remember people who improve after feedback.

e2.text: The feedback stays unresolved. Try again: thank, clarify, summarise, act.

quiz.q: Best first response to critical feedback?
options: Pause, thank, and ask for specific examples

quiz.q: Which question gets more useful feedback?
options: 'What would make this document a 9 out of 10?'

quiz.q: Which is NOT legitimate feedback?
options: Mocking your accent or region in front of the team
quiz.why: Humiliation and identity-based comments are mistreatment, not feedback.

quiz.q: After acting on feedback, a smart move is to…
options: Ask for a follow-up check in a few weeks
quiz.why: Follow-up shows ownership and confirms improvement.

lessons.title: Your offer letter, CTC and payslip (India)

story.title: Why is my salary less than I expected?

scenes.text: Fatima's offer letter from a Bengaluru firm says CTC ₹6,00,000. She divides by 12 and expects ₹50,000 a month.
Her first credit is much lower. She panics that there's a mistake.
Her friend in finance walks her through the payslip: employer PF, gratuity, variable pay, insurance, professional tax, income tax (TDS).
Nothing was wrong — CTC is 'cost to company', not 'cash in hand'. Next time she compares offers on take-home and benefits, not just CTC.

steps.title: CTC is not take-home
steps.body:
**CTC (Cost to Company)** is everything the employer spends on you in a year. It can include:
- **Fixed pay:** basic salary, HRA (house rent allowance), special allowance and others.
- **Employer's PF contribution.**
- **Gratuity** provision (paid only if you become eligible, usually after years of continuous service).
- **Variable pay / performance bonus** (often paid annually and depends on ratings and company results).
- **Insurance** premiums, meal cards, and other benefits.

Your **in-hand (net) monthly pay** = monthly gross pay minus deductions such as **employee PF**, **professional tax** (in states that levy it), and **income tax deducted at source (TDS)**.

steps.title: PF in one minute
steps.body: Under the EPF scheme, you and your employer each typically contribute **12% of your basic wages** (plus DA, if any). Part of the employer share goes to the pension scheme (EPS). Your **UAN (Universal Account Number)** stays the same across jobs — use it to transfer your PF when you switch rather than withdrawing it. Details and limits can change; check the EPFO portal or your HR for current rules.

steps.title: Worked example (illustrative numbers only)
steps.body:
Suppose CTC ₹6,00,000 includes ₹60,000 variable pay, ₹21,600 employer PF, ₹14,400 gratuity provision and ₹8,000 insurance.
- Fixed gross = 6,00,000 − 60,000 − 21,600 − 14,400 − 8,000 = **₹4,96,000 a year ≈ ₹41,333 a month**.
- Deductions per month: employee PF ₹1,800, professional tax ~₹200, TDS depends on your regime and declarations.
- In-hand ≈ ₹39,000 before tax.

The exact split varies by company — always ask HR for a **salary break-up** before accepting an offer.

steps.title: Documents to keep forever
steps.body:
- Offer letter, appointment letter and any revision letters.
- Payslips (at least the last few years) and **Form 16** (annual TDS certificate) for filing your income tax return.
- Relieving and experience letters from every employer (needed for background verification at the next job).
- PF passbook / UAN details.

Also choose your tax regime and submit investment declarations when HR asks — slabs and rules change in Union Budgets, so check the current ones on the Income Tax Department's site.

steps.title: Read before you sign
steps.body: Check: joining date, location and transfer clause, notice period, bond or training-cost recovery clauses, probation period, and variable-pay conditions. If a clause is unclear, ask HR in writing. *This is general education, not legal or tax advice.*

activity.prompt: An offer has CTC ₹8,40,000, which includes ₹84,000 variable pay, ₹28,800 employer PF, ₹19,200 gratuity provision and ₹12,000 insurance. What is the fixed gross pay per MONTH (before employee deductions)?

quiz.q: CTC stands for…
quiz.why: It's the total annual cost to the employer, not take-home.

quiz.q: Why is in-hand pay lower than CTC/12?
options: CTC includes employer PF, gratuity, variable pay and benefits; plus deductions like employee PF and TDS
quiz.why: Several CTC components aren't monthly cash.

quiz.q: What should you do with your UAN when switching jobs?
options: Use the same UAN and transfer PF
quiz.why: UAN is portable; transferring preserves savings and service continuity.

quiz.q: Form 16 is…
options: The employer's annual TDS certificate used for filing tax returns
quiz.why: It summarises salary and tax deducted.

questions.q: Many Indian companies align appraisal cycles with…
A 'wins log' is…
options: A weekly record of achievements with evidence

questions.q: CTC means…
options: Total annual cost to the employer

questions.q: Which line belongs in a strong self-assessment?
options: 'Cut report time from 3 hours to 20 minutes by automating it'

questions.q: Calibration exists to…
Under EPF, employee and employer each typically contribute…
questions.why: 12% each is the standard rate; check current rules.

questions.q: Best response when feedback stings?
Which is mistreatment rather than feedback?
options: Comments mocking your caste or region

questions.q: Variable pay usually depends on…
questions.why: It's performance-linked and may not be paid in full.

questions.q: CTC ₹6,00,000 including ₹60,000 variable, ₹21,600 employer PF, ₹14,400 gratuity, ₹8,000 insurance. Fixed gross per year is…
Under a guided distribution, why is documented impact especially important?
options: Because ratings are partly comparative across peers
questions.why: Managers must defend ratings with evidence in calibration.

questions.q: Which offer-letter clause most needs checking before signing?
questions.why: These have financial and career consequences.

questions.q: A balanced self-assessment includes…
options: 3–5 evidence-backed achievements plus 1–2 growth areas with a plan

corporate-politics-india.title: Office politics in Indian workplaces
corporate-politics-india.description: Real Indian office situations — credit stealing, the manager's favourite, 'sir/ma'am' hierarchy, festival vs deadline, WFH visibility, appraisal season, toxic peers, cliques, gossip, escalations and resignations — practised through branching scenarios with ethical, practical guidance.

courses.title: Office politics 101: credit, favourites and gossip
courses.summary: Understand workplace politics as the reality of influence, not dirty tricks — and practise handling credit stealing, the manager's favourite and office gossip ethically.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish healthy influence from manipulation
Learners can protect credit for their work without drama
Learners can respond to perceived favouritism constructively
Learners can stay out of gossip while staying connected

scenes.text: Tanvi, a data analyst in Hyderabad, proudly says, 'I don't do politics. My work speaks for itself.' She avoids lunch groups and never talks to anyone outside her team.
When a reorganisation happens, nobody in leadership knows her name. Her best project is presented by someone else's manager.
Her mentor, Ramesh, explains: 'Politics is just how decisions get made among people. You can do it ethically — by being known, trusted and useful.'
Tanvi starts sharing short monthly updates and helping other teams with data. Within a year, she is the person leaders ask for.

steps.title: Politics = influence + relationships + information
steps.body:
Whenever people with different goals share limited resources (budget, promotions, attention), there is politics. It exists in every country and every company — in a 20-person startup and in a 3-lakh-employee IT services firm.

Think of three kinds of behaviour:
- **Healthy influence:** building relationships, making your work visible, understanding stakeholders, persuading with data.
- **Defensive survival:** documenting agreements, clarifying credit, avoiding traps.
- **Toxic politics:** lying, taking credit, spreading rumours, sabotage, favouritism based on caste, region or personal loyalty.

The goal of this course: **get good at the first two, never do the third, and know how to respond when others do.**

steps.title: Why it can feel stronger in Indian workplaces
steps.body:
Some patterns common in many (not all) Indian organisations:
- **High respect for hierarchy** — seniors' opinions often carry extra weight; juniors may hesitate to disagree openly.
- **Relationship-driven work** — who you know (and who vouches for you) can matter as much as formal process.
- **Large teams and pyramids** — many freshers, fewer senior roles, so promotions are competitive.
- **Collective identity** — college, region, language, or previous-company groups form naturally.

None of these are bad in themselves. They become harmful when they replace fairness.

steps.title: The stakeholder map
steps.body:
Draw a 2×2: **influence over your work** (high/low) vs **interest in your work** (high/low).
- High influence, high interest (your manager, skip manager): **manage closely** — regular updates.
- High influence, low interest (a director in another function): **keep satisfied** — brief, occasional, relevant updates.
- Low influence, high interest (peers who depend on you): **keep informed.**
- Low/low: **monitor.**

This simple tool, borrowed from project management, is the ethical core of 'office politics'.

steps.title: Three ethical habits that beat politics
steps.body:
- **Be reliably useful** — deliver what you promise, when you promise.
- **Be visible** — short written updates; speak in meetings; share learnings.
- **Be fair** — give credit generously, don't gossip, keep confidences. Over years, a reputation for fairness is a strong form of power.

activity.prompt: Sort each behaviour.

items.text: Sending your manager a monthly impact summary
Confirming a verbal agreement by email
Presenting a teammate's analysis as your own
Helping another team with a data problem
Spreading a rumour that a peer is leaving
Keeping notes of who agreed to what in meetings
Favouring people from your home state in task allocation

quiz.q: Which is the healthiest definition of office politics?
options: How influence, relationships and information shape decisions
quiz.why: Politics is a neutral reality; your methods make it ethical or toxic.

quiz.q: In a stakeholder map, your skip-level manager is usually…
options: High influence — manage closely or keep satisfied

quiz.q: Why did Tanvi's 'work speaks for itself' approach fail?
options: Decision-makers didn't know her or her work
quiz.why: Work needs to be visible to the people deciding.

quiz.q: Confirming a verbal agreement by email is…
quiz.why: It prevents later 'I never agreed' disputes, when done politely.

scenes.text: Vivek, a junior analyst in Gurugram, spends two weeks building a churn dashboard. His senior colleague Sameer presents it to the VP: 'I built this to track churn.'
The VP praises Sameer. Vivek sits in the meeting, stunned and silent.
Vivek wants to reply-all to the VP with 'Actually, I built it.' His friend stops him.
Instead, he uses a calmer, smarter approach — and a month later the VP is calling him directly for analysis.

steps.title: First, check: theft or omission?
steps.body:
Credit 'stealing' ranges from **careless omission** (a senior says 'we' or forgets names under time pressure) to **deliberate theft** (repeatedly presenting your work as theirs). Respond in proportion.

Ask yourself: Is this the first time? Did they say 'I' or 'we'? Is your manager aware of your work? Your response should escalate only as the pattern becomes clearer.

steps.title: Prevent it: make authorship visible
steps.body:
- Put your name and date on documents (*'Prepared by Vivek Rao, 12 Aug'*).
- Share work with your manager first, in writing: *'Sharing the churn dashboard I built — key insight: churn is 2× higher in month 3.'*
- Present your own work when possible: *'Would it help if I walk the VP through it for five minutes?'*
- Post progress in team channels — this creates a natural, timestamped record.

steps.title: Worked example: the calm private conversation
steps.body:
Vivek to Sameer, privately: *'Sameer, I noticed in the VP review the dashboard was presented as built by you. I spent two weeks on it, so it matters to me that my contribution is visible. In future reviews, could we present it together, or could you mention my part?'*

No accusations, a specific fact, why it matters, and a specific request. Many people correct course after this. If it happens again, speak to your manager with facts and dates — not emotion.

steps.title: What not to do
steps.body:
- Public confrontation in front of the VP or reply-all corrections — you'll look petty even if you're right.
- Taking revenge by withholding help or data.
- Complaining in gossip circles — it reaches the person, distorted.
- And on the other side: **never take credit yourself.** Say 'Priya built this model; I'll explain how we used it.' Generous credit makes you look like a leader.

a.text: In a meeting with the director, your team lead presents your analysis and says, 'I found that delays are mostly in vendor approvals.' Everyone nods. What do you do in the meeting?

choices.label: Stay calm; add a useful detail: 'In the data I pulled, 62% of delays were in two vendors — happy to share the breakdown.'
choices.feedback: You've shown authorship by adding value, not by fighting.

choices.label: Interrupt: 'Actually that was MY analysis!'
choices.feedback: Accurate but publicly embarrassing to your lead; this usually backfires.

choices.label: Say nothing and fume
choices.feedback: Silence is safe for now, but the pattern may continue.

b.text: The director asks you to send the breakdown. After the meeting, what next?

choices.label: Email the breakdown to the director, cc your lead, with a short summary
choices.feedback: Creates a visible, polite record of your work.

choices.label: Send it secretly to the director only
choices.feedback: Going around your lead can damage trust; cc them.

c.text: The room goes silent. Your lead looks embarrassed and angry. Later, what do you do?

choices.label: Apologise for the delivery, then calmly explain why credit matters to you
choices.feedback: Repairs the relationship while keeping your point.

choices.label: Ignore your lead for a week
choices.feedback: Cold wars hurt you more than them.

d.text: Two days later, it happens again in a client update. What now?

choices.label: Have a calm private talk with your lead: fact, impact, request
choices.feedback: Right step once you see a pattern.

choices.label: Complain about your lead in the cafeteria
choices.feedback: Gossip spreads and makes you look unprofessional.

e1.text: The director now knows your name and work, and your lead isn't humiliated. This is ethical politics at its best.

e2.text: You got visibility, but your lead may see it as going behind their back. Transparency (cc) is safer.

e3.text: Your lead agrees to mention your contributions. If it repeats, take facts and dates to your manager or skip-level.

e4.text: The relationship sours and your reputation suffers. Prefer private, factual conversations.

quiz.q: Best way to prevent credit theft?
options: Make authorship visible: names on documents, written updates, presenting your own work

quiz.q: A first-time 'we did this' from your lead is most likely…
quiz.why: Escalate only as a pattern becomes clear.

quiz.q: A good private conversation about credit includes…
options: A specific fact, why it matters, and a specific request

quiz.q: How do leaders build reputation through credit?
quiz.why: Generous credit signals confidence and fairness.

quiz.q: If credit theft repeats after you've spoken privately, next step?
options: Take facts and dates to your manager or skip-level
quiz.why: Documented escalation through the right channel.

scenes.text: Kunal plays cricket with manager Deepak every weekend. He gets the best projects and the client trip to Singapore. Shalini, equally good, gets maintenance work.
Shalini tells her colleagues, 'It's all chamchagiri (sucking up).' She becomes cynical and does the minimum.
Her mentor asks two questions: 'Does Deepak know what you want? Have you shown him you can do it?' Shalini realises she has never asked.
She asks for a stretch project with a clear plan. She gets the next client migration — and later learns Kunal had volunteered for every tough assignment for a year.

steps.title: Is it favouritism or familiarity?
steps.body:
Managers give opportunities to people they **know, trust and see**. Sometimes that is unfair favouritism (based on caste, region, language, gender, personal loyalty or social life). Often it is **familiarity**: the favourite communicates more, volunteers more, or has a track record the manager has seen.

Before concluding it's unfair, check:
- Have I told my manager clearly what I want?
- Have I shown evidence I'm ready?
- Does the favourite do something visible I don't?

steps.title: Worked example: asking for opportunity
steps.body:
Shalini in her 1:1: *'Deepak, I'd like to work on a client-facing migration in the next quarter. I've handled the database maintenance for six months with zero P1 incidents, and I've completed the cloud migration course. What would you need to see from me to be considered for the next one?'*

This converts a grievance into a clear ask with evidence — and the last question makes the manager commit to criteria.

steps.title: When it really is unfair
steps.body:
If you see a real pattern — opportunities and ratings consistently going to one group regardless of performance, or decisions linked to caste, religion, region, gender or personal favours:
- Document specific instances (dates, assignments, outcomes).
- Seek a skip-level conversation or HR business partner discussion, focusing on fair process.
- Use the company's ethics or grievance channel if needed; many companies have whistle-blower policies.
- Build a network outside your manager — mentors, other teams — so one person doesn't control your whole career.

steps.title: Don't become bitter
steps.body: Cynicism ('everything is politics, why try?') hurts you most. Keep doing visible good work, keep relationships with the favourite civil (they may be your manager one day), and if the environment stays unfair, an internal transfer or a job change is a legitimate choice.

a.text: The manager's favourite gets the high-visibility project again. You feel overlooked. What's your first step?

choices.label: Ask your manager in a 1:1 what you'd need to show to be considered next time
choices.feedback: Turns frustration into a clear, fair ask.

choices.label: Tell colleagues the favourite is a chamcha
choices.feedback: Gossip spreads and labels you as negative.

choices.label: Quietly reduce your effort
choices.feedback: This confirms the manager's choice.

b.text: Manager: 'I need someone who can handle client calls confidently.' What do you do?

choices.label: Ask to shadow two client calls and present a small update yourself
choices.feedback: You've created a path to prove readiness.

choices.label: Say 'I can do it' and nothing more
choices.feedback: Without a plan, nothing changes.

c.text: A month later, your manager seems colder. What now?

choices.label: Reset: have the 1:1 conversation about opportunities and readiness
choices.feedback: It's never too late to switch to a constructive approach.

choices.label: Escalate to HR saying the manager is biased, without any examples
choices.feedback: Escalation needs evidence; vague complaints rarely help.

e1.text: After two shadowed calls and one presentation, you're on the next client project. Familiarity can be built.

e2.text: Your manager nods but nothing changes. Come back with a concrete plan.

e3.text: HR asks for specific examples you don't have. Document patterns first; real unfairness deserves a well-evidenced complaint.

quiz.q: Before concluding favouritism, you should check…
options: Whether you have clearly asked and shown readiness
quiz.why: Often the gap is communication and visibility.

quiz.q: Which question makes a manager commit to criteria?
options: 'What would you need to see from me to be considered next time?'

quiz.q: Real unfair favouritism should be handled by…
options: Documenting instances and using skip-level, HR or ethics channels

quiz.q: Why build a network beyond your manager?
options: So one person doesn't control your whole career
quiz.why: Mentors and other teams open doors.

lessons.title: Office gossip: stay connected, stay clean

scenes.text: At the 4 pm chai break, colleagues whisper that Leena from finance was 'caught' and is being fired. Everyone looks at Abhishek, the new joiner, to see if he'll add anything.
By evening, the rumour is in three WhatsApp groups with new details.
The truth: Leena had taken medical leave for surgery. She returns to find people avoiding her.
Abhishek, who had said only 'I don't know anything about it', is one of the few she still trusts.

steps.title: Information vs gossip
steps.body:
Not all informal talk is bad. **Useful informal information**: 'The VP prefers one-page summaries', 'Finance closes books on the 25th.' **Gossip**: speculation about people's personal lives, health, relationships, salaries, conflicts, or who will be fired.

Test: *Would I say this if the person were standing here? Is it true, kind and necessary?*

steps.title: How to exit gossip without being 'boring'
steps.body:
- **Redirect:** *'No idea — by the way, did anyone try the new canteen thali?'*
- **Neutral fact:** *'I heard she's on leave; hope she's okay.'*
- **Gentle boundary:** *'I'd rather not guess about that.'*
- **Leave:** *'Got a call — catch you later.'*

You don't need to lecture anyone. Just don't add fuel.

steps.title: Digital gossip is permanent
steps.body: WhatsApp forwards and chat screenshots last forever and can be shown to HR. Spreading false information about a colleague can lead to disciplinary action, and posting confidential company information can breach your employment terms. Health information about colleagues is especially sensitive — never share it.

steps.title: Be the vault
steps.body: People quietly notice who keeps confidences. Over time, the person who doesn't leak becomes the one people trust with real information — which is real influence. If a colleague confides something serious (harassment, mental health crisis), listen, keep it private, and encourage them toward the right support (HR, POSH committee, EAP, Tele-MANAS 14416) — and seek help urgently if anyone's safety is at risk (112).

a.text: In a team WhatsApp group someone posts: 'Heard Rohan got a PIP, he's definitely out by March 😂'. What do you do?

choices.label: Don't react; if it continues, message the poster privately: 'Not cool to post about Rohan here.'
choices.feedback: A private nudge stops spread without public drama.

choices.label: Reply 'lol I knew it'
choices.feedback: You've added fuel and your name is now on the screenshot.

choices.label: Forward it to your friend in another team
choices.feedback: Spreading it makes you part of the problem.

b.text: The poster replies, 'Relax, just joking.' Rohan is in the group. What next?

choices.label: Check in privately with Rohan: 'Saw that message — hope you're okay. Anything I can help with?'
choices.feedback: Support without prying.

choices.label: Leave it there
choices.feedback: Acceptable, but a kind word could matter a lot to Rohan.

c.text: Rohan sees the chat and complains to HR with screenshots. HR asks you about your reply. What do you say?

choices.label: Admit it, apologise to Rohan, and commit not to repeat it
choices.feedback: Owning it is the only good option now.

choices.label: Claim your phone was hacked
choices.feedback: Lying makes it far worse.

e1.text: Rohan thanks you. Kindness during someone's hard time is remembered for years.

e2.text: You stayed clean. Next time consider a quiet word of support.

e3.text: You receive a warning but keep your credibility by owning it. Lesson learned: screenshots are forever.

e4.text: HR doesn't believe you. A small mistake has become a dishonesty issue.

quiz.q: Which is useful informal information, not gossip?
A graceful way to exit gossip is…
Why is digital gossip especially risky?
options: Screenshots are permanent and can reach HR
quiz.why: Written records persist and can be used in disciplinary processes.

quiz.q: A colleague confides about harassment. You should…
options: Listen, keep it private, and point them to POSH/HR support
quiz.why: Confidential support and correct channels protect them.

questions.q: Office politics is best described as…
options: How influence and relationships shape decisions

questions.q: Which is toxic politics?
A gossip test question is…
options: Is it true, kind and necessary?
questions.why: Simple filter for what to share.

questions.q: High-influence, high-interest stakeholders should be…
Best in-meeting response when your work is presented by someone else?
options: Add a value detail showing you know the data, then follow up in writing

questions.q: Before calling something favouritism, check if you've…
Putting 'Prepared by' and a date on documents helps…
When following up with a director, why cc your lead?
options: Transparency avoids looking like you went behind their back

questions.q: Unfair favouritism based on region or caste should be…
options: Documented and raised through skip-level, HR or ethics channels

questions.q: Fact–impact–request means…
options: State what happened, why it matters, what you'd like next

questions.q: A colleague's health information you overheard should be…
Why is being 'the vault' a source of influence?
options: People trust those who keep confidences and share real information with them

questions.q: Your skip-level asks you directly whether your lead built the dashboard. Best answer?
options: Answer honestly and factually without attacking: 'I built it; my lead reviewed and presented it.'
questions.why: Honest, neutral facts protect both your integrity and relationships.
