Learners can respond to regional/language cliques inclusively
Learners can plan around festivals and family obligations professionally

scenes.text: Priyanka, a fresher in a Kolkata manufacturing firm, calls everyone 'sir' or 'ma'am'. In a review, she notices the plant head's estimate is off by a factor of ten — a unit mistake.
She stays silent. 'Who am I to correct sir?'
The wrong estimate goes into a purchase order. The error costs weeks to fix.
Her manager later tells her: 'Respect means telling me when I'm wrong — politely. Silence isn't respect.'

steps.title: Respect and hierarchy
steps.body:
Many Indian workplaces have a **high power-distance** culture: seniors are addressed formally, decisions flow top-down, and openly contradicting a senior can feel disrespectful. Global and startup teams often prefer first names and open debate.

Good rule: **follow the local norm for address, but never let formality stop you from raising important facts.** If your team uses first names, using 'sir' repeatedly may sound distant; if unsure, ask your buddy, or start formal and follow what seniors invite you to do (*'Please call me Ravi'*).

steps.title: Worked example: disagreeing respectfully
steps.body:
Phrases that keep respect and still deliver the fact:
- *'Sir, may I check one number? I think the quantity may be in kilograms rather than tonnes — could we verify before the PO goes out?'*
- *'I may be missing context, but the data I have shows something different — can I share it after the meeting?'*
- *'Could I offer a different view?'*

Notice: **question form, offer to verify, focus on data, not the person.** If the room is too formal, raise it right after the meeting, privately but quickly.

steps.title: Switching between cultures
steps.body: In a single day, an Indian engineer may talk to a formal plant head, a casual startup founder and an American client who wants direct pushback. Skilled professionals **code-switch**: formal address and indirect phrasing with traditional seniors; first names and direct 'I disagree, here's why' with global teams. Both are respectful within their context.

steps.title: When safety, money or ethics are involved
steps.body: If a mistake could hurt someone (safety), lose significant money, or break law or policy, **speak up even if it's uncomfortable** — and if ignored, escalate through the proper channel. 'I was only following sir's instructions' is not a defence for safety or ethics violations.

a.text: In a meeting, your senior VP says a project will cost ₹40 lakh. Your spreadsheet clearly shows ₹4 crore. Ten people are in the room. What do you do?

choices.label: Politely ask: 'Sir, may I check one figure? My sheet shows ₹4 crore — could we verify?'
choices.feedback: Respectful, factual and timely.

choices.label: Stay silent and send an email later
choices.feedback: Okay for small issues; for a 10× difference, raising it now or immediately after is better.

choices.label: Say 'That's wrong, you've made a mistake'
choices.feedback: The fact is right but the framing may embarrass a senior publicly.

b.text: The VP checks and says, 'You're right, good catch.' How do you follow up?

choices.label: Send the corrected sheet with the source after the meeting
choices.feedback: Closing the loop builds trust.

c.text: You email the VP right after the meeting. But the figure was already shared with the board. What now?

choices.label: Email clearly with the data and offer to help correct it quickly
choices.feedback: Still the right move; next time raise big issues in the room.

d.text: The VP looks irritated: 'Let's discuss later.' What do you do?

choices.label: Meet after, apologise for how you said it, and walk through the data
choices.feedback: Separating the delivery from the fact repairs it.

choices.label: Drop it to avoid conflict
choices.feedback: The wrong number goes forward — the worst outcome.

e1.text: You saved the project from a 10× error and earned a reputation for careful, respectful courage.

e2.text: The error is fixed. Lesson: speak early, politely, with data.

e3.text: The wrong estimate causes serious problems later. Silence was not respect.

quiz.q: High power-distance culture means…
options: Hierarchy is strongly respected and juniors may hesitate to disagree
quiz.why: It shapes how disagreement is expressed.

quiz.q: Which phrase disagrees respectfully?
options: 'May I check one number? My data shows something different.'
quiz.why: Question form plus data keeps respect.

quiz.q: When must you speak up even if uncomfortable?
options: When safety, significant money or ethics are involved
quiz.why: Following instructions is no defence for harm.

quiz.q: 'Code-switching' at work means…
options: Adjusting formality and directness to the context
quiz.why: Respect looks different in different cultures.

lessons.title: Saying no to an elder colleague

scenes.text: Mr Sharma, 52, a respected senior accountant in a Jaipur firm, asks 25-year-old Neeraj to 'just quickly' prepare his monthly reconciliation — again.
Neeraj has done it four times. His own GST filing work is now late, and his manager has noticed.
Saying no to someone his father's age feels deeply wrong to Neeraj.
He learns to say a respectful 'no, but…' — and Sharma ji, surprisingly, takes it well.

steps.title: Respect the person, protect the priority
steps.body:
In Indian culture, elders are respected and refusing them can feel rude. But taking on unofficial work that delays your assigned priorities hurts you, your manager and eventually the elder too.

Key idea: **respect is in your tone and alternatives, not in automatic yes.** You can be warm and still decline.

steps.title: Worked example: four ways to say no respectfully
steps.body:
- **No + reason + alternative:** *'Sharma ji, I'd love to help, but the GST filing is due Friday and I'm behind. Could I show you the reconciliation template so it's quicker for you?'*
- **Not now:** *'I can't today — can I help on Monday afternoon?'*
- **Prioritise via manager:** *'Happy to, but my manager has asked me to finish the filing first. Shall I check with her whether this can take priority?'*
- **Teach instead of do:** offer a 20-minute walkthrough or a checklist.

Use respectful address (ji, sir), warm tone and a real alternative.

steps.title: When the 'favour' is a red flag
Keep the relationship warm
steps.body: After declining, keep the relationship strong: greet them, ask for their advice on something they know well, appreciate their experience. Elder colleagues often have deep institutional knowledge — a relationship worth more than a reconciliation sheet.

a.text: A senior colleague, 30 years older, asks you for the fifth time to do his weekly MIS report. Your own deadline is tomorrow. What do you say?

choices.label: 'I'd like to help, but my deadline is tomorrow. Can I show you a faster template on Thursday?'
choices.feedback: Respectful no with a real alternative.

choices.label: 'Yes sir' — and stay up till 2 am
choices.feedback: Your work suffers and the pattern continues.

choices.label: 'That's not my job.'
choices.feedback: True perhaps, but blunt; it may damage the relationship.

b.text: He frowns: 'In my days juniors helped seniors.' What now?

choices.label: Smile, stay warm: 'I really do want to help — Thursday I'll make sure it becomes a 10-minute job for you.'
choices.feedback: Calm consistency usually wins.

choices.label: Give in out of guilt
choices.feedback: Guilt-yes recreates the problem.

c.text: You miss your deadline; your manager asks why. What do you say?

choices.label: Explain honestly and ask how to handle such requests going forward
choices.feedback: Involving your manager makes future no's easier.

choices.label: Blame the senior colleague angrily
choices.feedback: Blame without having set a boundary looks unfair.

d.text: He's offended and complains you're arrogant. What do you do?

choices.label: Apologise for the tone, explain your deadline, offer the template help
choices.feedback: You can repair tone while keeping the boundary.

e1.text: He learns the template, the requests stop, and he still greets you warmly. Respect and boundaries can coexist.

e2.text: Your manager tells the senior that your priorities come first. Next time, set the boundary earlier.

e3.text: The relationship sours. A respectful no earlier would have avoided this.

quiz.q: Which is a respectful no?
options: 'I can't today because of my deadline — can I help Monday?'

quiz.q: An elder colleague asks for your password to 'save time'. You should…
options: Firmly decline; it violates security policy regardless of seniority
Write it on a sticky note

quiz.q: How can your manager help with repeated favours?
options: They can set priorities, which makes declining easier
quiz.why: Manager-set priorities give you legitimate cover.

quiz.q: 'Teach instead of do' means…
options: Offering a walkthrough or template so they can do it themselves
quiz.why: It helps once and solves the pattern.

story.title: Lunch in Tamil, meetings in Tamil

scenes.text: In a Chennai office, most of Kavya's team speaks Tamil at lunch and, increasingly, in meetings. Aakash from Lucknow and Ritika from Assam feel left out.
Decisions sometimes happen in quick Tamil side-conversations. Aakash misses context and his work suffers.
Kavya, who is Tamil herself, notices and starts gently switching meetings to English: 'Let's use English so everyone's in.'
Aakash starts learning a few Tamil phrases; the team enjoys teaching him. Lunch becomes a mix of languages and stories.

steps.title: Why cliques form
steps.body: People naturally bond over a shared language, region, food, college or previous company. It's comforting, especially for people far from home. The problem starts when cliques **exclude others from information and opportunities** — decisions in a language some can't follow, assignments going to 'our people', jokes about other regions.

steps.title: The work-language rule
steps.body:
A simple, widely used norm: **in work discussions, use the language everyone in the room understands** (often English in mixed teams). Social chats in a shared mother tongue are fine — but switch when someone joins, and never make work decisions in a language a team member can't follow.

If you're excluded: *'Sorry, could we switch to English? I want to make sure I don't miss anything.'* — said lightly, it rarely offends.

steps.title: Stereotypes are not jokes
steps.body: Jokes about someone's region, state, accent, food, skin colour, caste or religion can be deeply hurtful and may violate company policies on harassment and discrimination. Not every hurtful comment is meant to hurt, but impact matters. Simple response: *'Not cool, yaar.'* For repeated or serious cases, report to HR.

steps.title: Be a bridge
steps.body:
- If you're in the majority group, invite the newcomer to lunch and translate the context.
- If you're the outsider, show curiosity: learn greetings, try local food, share your own culture.
- Managers: rotate assignments transparently and run meetings in a common language. Diversity of backgrounds is a strength in teams that make everyone feel included.

a.text: Your team's planning call keeps drifting into Telugu. You don't speak it, and you've just realised a task deadline was moved without you knowing. What do you do?

choices.label: Lightly ask: 'Could we switch to English? I think I missed the deadline change.'
choices.feedback: Friendly and specific — this usually works immediately.

choices.label: Stay silent and complain to other non-Telugu colleagues
choices.feedback: Forming a counter-clique deepens the divide.

b.text: They apologise and switch. A week later it happens again. What next?

choices.label: Raise it with your manager as a process suggestion: 'Can we agree meetings are in English and decisions are posted in the channel?'
choices.feedback: Turns a personal frustration into a team norm.

choices.label: Accuse the team of being regionalist in the group chat
choices.feedback: Public accusation makes people defensive.

c.text: Two groups form. Collaboration drops. Your manager notices. What do you do?

choices.label: Suggest the common-language norm and written decisions to your manager
choices.feedback: Fixes the process rather than blaming people.

e1.text: The team agrees: meetings in English, decisions posted in the channel. Lunch stays multilingual and fun.

e2.text: Tension rises. Process suggestions work better than public accusations.

quiz.q: When do language cliques become a problem?
options: When they exclude people from work information or opportunities
quiz.why: Exclusion from work is the harm.

quiz.q: A good work-language norm is…
options: Use the language everyone in the room understands for work

quiz.q: A stereotype joke about someone's state is…
options: Potentially hurtful and may violate policy

quiz.q: A good way to bridge as an outsider?
options: Show curiosity: learn greetings, share your culture

lessons.title: Festival and family pressure vs deadlines

story.title: Diwali, a wedding, and a go-live

scenes.text: Harsh, from Indore, has booked tickets home for Diwali. His cousin's wedding is the same week. The client's go-live is suddenly moved to Diwali week.
His mother asks daily when he's coming. His manager asks who can support go-live.
Harsh plans: he finishes his handover early, agrees to be on-call for two hours on go-live day from home, and swaps with a colleague who will take Christmas off instead.
He attends the wedding, the go-live succeeds, and his manager notes his planning in the appraisal.

steps.title: Plan festivals like a project
steps.body:
India has many festivals and family events — Diwali, Eid, Pongal, Onam, Durga Puja, Christmas, Holi, weddings, and more — and teams are diverse, so someone is almost always celebrating something.
- Check the company holiday calendar and optional/restricted holidays at the start of the year.
- **Apply for leave early** and put it on the team calendar.
- Ask about release dates and peak periods before booking tickets.
- Offer swaps: colleagues who celebrate different festivals can cover for each other.

steps.title: Worked example: negotiating leave in a crunch
steps.body:
*'Rekha, my cousin's wedding is 10–14 Nov and I've had leave approved since August. I see go-live moved to 12 Nov. Here's my plan: I'll finish testing and the handover document by 8 Nov, Anil has agreed to be primary on go-live, and I can be on call 6–8 pm on the 12th. Does that work?'*

It states the facts, shows ownership, and offers a solution instead of just a problem.

steps.title: When work asks too much
steps.body:
Occasional crunch is normal; constant cancellation of approved leave is not. If it becomes a pattern:
- Document approved leaves and cancellations.
- Discuss with your manager calmly about planning and staffing.
- Know your company's leave policy and applicable law; HR can clarify.

Your family time and rest are not 'luxuries' — burnout harms both you and the work.

steps.title: Respect others' festivals
steps.body: Don't assume everyone celebrates what you do. Wish colleagues for their festivals, avoid scheduling key meetings on major festivals of team members, and be the one who volunteers to cover so others can go home — they'll return the favour.

a.text: Your Diwali leave was approved months ago. Two weeks before, your manager says, 'Client moved the release to Diwali week; can you cancel your leave?' What do you do?

choices.label: Propose a plan: early handover, a colleague as primary, limited on-call from home
choices.feedback: Solution-oriented and protects both priorities.

choices.label: Cancel immediately without discussing your family plans
choices.feedback: Sometimes needed, but you didn't explore options.

choices.label: Refuse flatly and stop replying
choices.feedback: Your leave is valid, but no discussion damages trust.

b.text: Manager: 'The client wants someone who knows the module.' What next?

choices.label: Offer a recorded walkthrough and an overlap session with the colleague
choices.feedback: Knowledge transfer makes your absence safe.

choices.label: Say 'Not my problem'
choices.feedback: Dismissive; keep collaborating.

c.text: Your family is upset. Next year the same thing happens. What now?

choices.label: Discuss with your manager how to plan releases and backups around festivals
choices.feedback: Fixing the process prevents repeats.

d.text: Your manager escalates, saying you're uncooperative. What can you do?

choices.label: Reopen the conversation with a concrete coverage plan
choices.feedback: It's never too late to propose solutions.

e1.text: You celebrate with family; the release succeeds with your colleague. Your planning is remembered.

e2.text: The team now plans backups for each festival. Occasional sacrifices become rare.

quiz.q: The best time to apply for festival leave is…
options: After booking non-refundable tickets without telling anyone
As early as possible, after checking release dates

quiz.q: A strong leave negotiation includes…
options: Facts, ownership, a coverage plan and limited availability if needed

quiz.q: If approved leave is repeatedly cancelled, you should…
options: Document, discuss planning and staffing, and know the policy

quiz.q: A culturally respectful habit is…
options: Covering for colleagues during their festivals
Scheduling key meetings on colleagues' major festivals

questions.q: Respect in hierarchical cultures is shown mainly through…
options: Tone, address and how you raise issues

questions.q: A respectful no includes…
In mixed teams, work meetings should use…
Apply for festival leave…
options: Early, and add it to team calendars

questions.q: Which senior request must you refuse?
If excluded by a language switch, a good response is…
options: 'Could we switch to English so I don't miss anything?'

questions.q: Which phrasing best corrects a senior in public?
options: 'May I verify one figure? My data shows ₹4 crore.'

questions.q: Following a senior's unsafe instruction is…
options: Not a defence; raise and escalate safety, money or ethics issues
questions.why: Speak up on safety and ethics.

questions.q: Asking a manager to set priorities when an elder keeps adding work…
options: Gives you legitimate cover to decline

questions.q: Stereotype jokes about regions may…
Best long-term fix for festival-week release clashes?
options: Plan releases and backups around festivals as a team process
Hire only people who don't celebrate

questions.q: A new teammate keeps calling you 'sir' though your team uses first names. Most helpful response?
options: Warmly invite them to use your first name and explain the team norm
questions.why: Seniors set the norm by invitation.

questions.q: Code-switching between a formal plant head and a direct US client is…
options: A skill: adjusting style while keeping content honest

courses.title: Visibility, appraisal season, toxic peers and exits
courses.summary: Stay visible while working from home, navigate appraisal-season politics, handle toxic peers and escalations, and resign gracefully with good notice-period etiquette.
outcomes: Learners can make remote work visible without 'performing busy'
Learners can navigate appraisal season with evidence and calm
Learners can handle a toxic peer and escalate correctly
Learners can resign professionally, serve notice and leave on good terms

scenes.text: Rizwan works from home in Lucknow for a Bengaluru team. He keeps his Teams status green all day, even moving his mouse to stay 'active'.
Office-going colleagues chat with the manager at the coffee machine and get the interesting tasks.
His manager says in a review: 'I don't really know what you've delivered this quarter.'
Rizwan switches from 'looking busy' to 'showing outcomes': a Friday summary, demos and quick calls. His next review is the best of his career.

steps.title: Outcomes beat online status
steps.body:
Many hybrid teams show **proximity bias** — people who are physically present can get more attention and opportunities. Fighting it with a permanently green status or fake activity doesn't work; managers notice results, not dots.

Instead, make **outcomes visible**:
- A short **Friday update**: 3 wins, 1–2 next priorities, any blockers.
- **Demos** of finished work in team meetings.
- **Written decisions** in shared channels.

steps.title: Worked example: a Friday update
steps.body:
*'Week of 14 July — Rizwan*
- *Done: payment retry live; failed payments down from 4.1% to 2.6% (first 3 days).*
- *Done: reviewed 6 PRs for the new joiners.*
- *Next: refund API design doc (draft by Wed).*
- *Blocker: need sandbox keys from the bank — raised ticket SR-221.'*

Two minutes to read, impossible to ignore.

steps.title: Remote presence habits
steps.body:
- Cameras on for 1:1s and key meetings (when possible).
- Speak in the first 10 minutes of meetings.
- Schedule a 15-minute virtual chai with teammates every couple of weeks.
- Visit the office for important events (planning, offsites) if feasible.
- Be responsive within agreed hours; agree on 'core hours' with your team.

steps.title: Don't do this
steps.body: Mouse-jigglers and fake activity can breach company policy and destroy trust if discovered. Moonlighting (a second job) without permission can breach your employment contract and has led to terminations in Indian IT. Always check your company's policies.

a.text: You're fully remote. Your manager just gave a high-profile task to an office-based colleague, saying 'He was right there.' What do you do?

choices.label: In your next 1:1, say you'd like such tasks and agree how to make your work visible
choices.feedback: Constructive and specific.

choices.label: Keep your status green 14 hours a day
choices.feedback: Activity isn't impact; you'll burn out.

choices.label: Complain in the team chat about office favouritism
choices.feedback: Public complaints make people defensive.

b.text: Manager agrees and asks what would help. What do you propose?

choices.label: A Friday update, demos in team meetings, and being pinged for urgent tasks
choices.feedback: Concrete visibility plan.

choices.label: Daily 1-hour calls with the manager
choices.feedback: Too heavy; keep it light and useful.

c.text: A month later you're exhausted and still not getting key tasks. What now?

choices.label: Switch to outcome-based updates and have the 1:1 conversation
choices.feedback: Better late than never.

d.text: Your manager messages you privately, irritated. What now?

choices.label: Apologise for posting publicly and request a 1:1 to discuss opportunities
choices.feedback: Repair, then constructive ask.

e1.text: Your work becomes visible; you get the next high-profile task. Remote doesn't mean invisible.

e2.text: Manager says that's too much; you settle on a weekly update. Keep it light.

quiz.q: Proximity bias means…
options: Preferring people who sit physically closer or are present more
quiz.why: Hybrid teams must counter it deliberately.

quiz.q: The best way to be visible remotely is…
options: Showing outcomes: updates, demos, written decisions

quiz.q: A good Friday update contains…
Undisclosed moonlighting may…
options: Breach your employment contract and lead to termination

story.title: March in a Pune IT office

scenes.text: It's March. Suddenly, everyone is volunteering, sending appreciation emails and attending every meeting. Jyoti calls it 'appraisal season theatre'.
Her colleague Manish gets a better rating despite, she feels, weaker work. Jyoti wants to fight her 'Meets' rating.
She instead prepares evidence: three outcomes with numbers, client appreciation, and her goals sheet.
Her rating isn't changed this year, but her manager commits to a growth plan and a mid-year check — and she gets 'Exceeds' the next cycle.

steps.title: Why the theatre happens
steps.body: Recency bias is real: managers remember the last few weeks more vividly. That's why people become hyper-visible in appraisal season. The ethical counter is **steady visibility all year** (wins log, monthly updates) plus a strong self-assessment — not last-minute performance.

steps.title: Discussing a rating you disagree with
steps.body:
- **Wait a day** before reacting.
- Ask for the **reasoning and evidence**: *'Could you help me understand which goals you felt I didn't fully meet?'*
- Present **your evidence calmly**, tied to goals.
- Ask about **process**: is there a review or appeal mechanism?
- Focus on **next cycle**: *'What specifically would 'Exceeds' look like for me next year? Can we check in at mid-year?'*

Ratings are rarely changed after calibration, but a well-handled conversation shapes the next year.

steps.title: Avoid these
steps.body:
- Comparing your rating with colleagues' by name (*'Manish got Exceeds!'*) — you don't know their goals, and it sounds petty.
- Threatening to resign unless you have an offer and truly intend to leave.
- Badmouthing the manager to the skip-level in anger.
- Lobbying peers to give you favourable 360° feedback.

steps.title: If you're a strong performer every year but stuck
steps.body: If evidence-based conversations repeatedly don't work, ask a skip-level or mentor for perspective, consider an internal move, or test the market. Staying where your work isn't valued is a choice, not an obligation.

a.text: You receive 'Meets Expectations'. You expected 'Exceeds'. Your manager asks, 'Any questions?' What do you say right now?

choices.label: 'I'd like to understand the reasoning. Could we talk tomorrow after I've reflected?'
choices.feedback: Calm and buys time to prepare.

choices.label: 'This is unfair! Manish got Exceeds!'
choices.feedback: Comparisons sound petty and derail the talk.

b.text: Next day: you bring evidence. Your manager says calibration is final. What next?

choices.label: Ask what 'Exceeds' would look like next year and request a mid-year check
choices.feedback: You've turned a loss into a clear plan.

choices.label: Say you'll resign
choices.feedback: An empty threat weakens your position.

c.text: Your manager becomes defensive. The talk ends badly. What can you do?

choices.label: Apologise for the comparison and ask to discuss evidence and next-year goals
choices.feedback: Repair and redirect.

e1.text: With clear criteria and a mid-year check, you get 'Exceeds' next cycle.

e2.text: Your manager says, 'That's your choice.' Never threaten what you don't plan to do.

quiz.q: Recency bias in appraisals means…
options: Remembering the most recent weeks more

quiz.q: Best first response to a disappointing rating?
options: Ask to discuss reasoning after reflecting

quiz.q: Why avoid comparing your rating with a named colleague?
options: You don't know their goals and it sounds petty

quiz.q: If calibration is final, focus on…
options: Clear criteria for next year and a mid-year check

scenes.text: Nitin, a peer in a Mumbai ad agency, interrupts Aditi in every meeting, mocks her ideas ('very creative, very useless') and blames her when deadlines slip.
Aditi starts dreading Mondays.
A senior advises: talk to Nitin directly once, document everything, then escalate with facts if it continues.
After a calm direct talk fails, Aditi brings a dated log to her manager. The manager intervenes; Nitin's behaviour changes.

steps.title: Difficult vs toxic
steps.body: **Difficult**: blunt, disorganised, different working style — irritating but not harmful. **Toxic**: repeated undermining, public humiliation, blame-shifting, sabotage, exclusion, threats. Harassment linked to gender, caste, religion, disability or other identity is more serious still and should go to HR (and the Internal Committee under POSH if sexual in nature).

steps.title: Step 1: a direct, private conversation
steps.body:
Use **SBI (Situation–Behaviour–Impact)**:
*'Nitin, in yesterday's client prep (situation), you interrupted me three times and called my idea useless in front of the team (behaviour). It made it hard for me to contribute and it looked bad to the client team (impact). I'd like us to let each other finish and disagree on ideas, not people. Can we agree on that?'*

Calm, specific, about behaviour — not character ('you're a bully').

steps.title: Step 2: document
steps.body: Keep a private log (not on a shared company drive others can access): date, what happened, exact words if possible, witnesses, impact on work, any messages. Save emails and chat links. Facts over feelings: *'12 Mar, 11:15 standup: said "very creative, very useless" about my proposal; Ravi and Sana present.'*

steps.title: Step 3: escalate the right way
steps.body:
Typical order: **your manager → skip-level or HR business partner → formal grievance/ethics channel**. For sexual harassment, go to the **Internal Committee** under the POSH Act. When you escalate:
- Lead with impact on work and team.
- Bring the log.
- State what you've already tried.
- Ask for a specific outcome (mediation, meeting norms, change of reporting).

An **escalation is not snitching** — it's using the system designed for this.

steps.title: Protect your wellbeing
steps.body: Limit 1:1 time with the person, keep interactions in writing when possible, and lean on supportive colleagues. If it's affecting your sleep or health, talk to someone — EAP if available, or Tele-MANAS (14416).

a.text: A peer blames you in front of your manager for a delay he caused. You have the email proving he delivered late. What now?

choices.label: Calmly state the fact in the meeting: 'I received the input on 14 March; I'll share the thread.'
choices.feedback: Neutral facts, no attack.

choices.label: Attack: 'You're lying as usual!'
choices.feedback: Personal attacks make you look like part of the problem.

choices.label: Say nothing
choices.feedback: The false narrative may stick.

b.text: You share the thread. Your peer continues sniping in later meetings. Next step?

choices.label: Have a private SBI conversation with him
choices.feedback: Give direct resolution one fair try.

choices.label: Go straight to HR with a long complaint
choices.feedback: Possible, but a direct conversation or manager first is usually expected unless it's harassment.

c.text: Your manager calls you both in; you're both told to 'behave'. What now?

choices.label: Apologise for your tone, then share facts privately with the manager
choices.feedback: Separate tone from facts.

d.text: Your manager seems to believe the peer. What can you still do?

choices.label: Send your manager the email thread with a neutral note
choices.feedback: Facts in writing correct the record.

e.text: He laughs it off and continues. You've logged five incidents. Next?

choices.label: Escalate to your manager with the log, impact and what you've tried
choices.feedback: Exactly the right escalation.

f.text: HR asks whether you've raised it with him or your manager. You haven't. What do you do?

choices.label: Agree to try the manager route first while HR keeps a note
choices.feedback: Following the process helps your case.

g.text: Your manager sets meeting norms and talks to the peer; behaviour improves. If not, the documented case moves to HR — and you're well prepared.

quiz.q: Which is 'toxic' rather than 'difficult'?
SBI stands for…
quiz.why: A structure for specific, non-personal feedback.

quiz.q: A good incident log includes…
Sexual harassment at work should go to…
options: The Internal Committee under the POSH Act

scenes.text: Amit gets a great offer and resigns by email at 11 pm with one line: 'I resign. Last day ASAP.' He mentally checks out and leaves no handover.
Swati gets an offer too. She tells her manager first in a 1:1, submits a formal letter, and builds a handover plan.
Two years later, Swati's old manager refers her for a senior role. Amit's background verification includes a lukewarm note and a delayed relieving letter.
The industry is smaller than it looks — especially in Indian tech hubs.

steps.title: Before you resign
steps.body:
- **Have a signed offer** (not just a verbal one) and ideally clear your background-verification documents.
- **Read your contract**: notice period (commonly 30–90 days in Indian corporate roles), buyout rules, leave adjustment, bond/clawback clauses (joining bonus, relocation, training costs).
- Know your **last working day** options: full notice, early release by mutual agreement, or buyout where permitted.

This is general education, not legal advice — check your own contract and HR policy.

steps.title: Worked example: telling your manager and the letter
steps.body:
**Tell your manager first, in person or on a call**, before HR or colleagues:
*'Priya, I wanted you to hear this from me first. I've accepted an offer and will be resigning. I've learned a lot here and want to make the transition smooth.'*

**Letter (short, positive, factual):**
*'Dear Priya, Please accept this as formal notice of my resignation from the role of Senior Analyst. As per my notice period of 60 days, my last working day will be 30 September. I will ensure a complete handover. Thank you for the opportunities and support. Regards, Swati'*

Submit it through the official HR system if there is one.

steps.title: Counter-offers and the notice period
steps.body:
Your company may make a **counter-offer**. Decide in advance what would make you stay — if the reasons you're leaving are not about money (growth, culture, manager), a raise often doesn't fix them. Never use a fake offer to get a raise; it can backfire badly.

During notice: keep working properly, write a **handover document** (ongoing tasks, contacts, passwords handed over through approved methods, known issues), train your replacement, don't take confidential data, and don't badmouth the company.

steps.title: Exit cleanly
steps.body:
- Collect your **relieving letter, experience letter, final settlement** details, and Form 16.
- Transfer **PF** using your UAN.
- In the exit interview, be honest but constructive.
- Send a warm goodbye note with your personal contact (LinkedIn). Thank people specifically.

Also: accepting an offer and then not joining ('ghosting') damages your reputation; if you change your mind, inform the new company promptly and politely.

scenes.text: Aditya runs operations for a Jaipur D2C clothing brand. Revenue grew 40% this year and the team celebrated.
The CFO says profit fell. Aditya is confused: 'How can we sell more and earn less?'
She walks him down the P&L: discounts and courier costs rose faster than sales, and marketing spend doubled.
Aditya now watches gross margin and contribution per order, not just revenue.

steps.title: The P&L ladder
steps.body:
A **profit and loss statement (P&L)** shows performance over a period (month, quarter, year):
- **Revenue** (sales, net of returns and discounts)
- − **Cost of goods sold (COGS)** — direct costs of what you sold (materials, manufacturing, direct labour)
- = **Gross profit** → *Gross margin % = gross profit ÷ revenue*
- − **Operating expenses (Opex)** — salaries, rent, marketing, software
- = **EBITDA** (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation)
- − **Depreciation & amortisation**
- = **EBIT / operating profit**
- − **Interest** − **Tax**
- = **Net profit (PAT, profit after tax)**

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Revenue ₹10 crore; COGS ₹6 crore → gross profit ₹4 crore (**40% gross margin**).
Opex ₹2.5 crore → EBITDA ₹1.5 crore (15%).
Depreciation ₹0.3 crore → EBIT ₹1.2 crore.
Interest ₹0.2 crore → profit before tax ₹1.0 crore.
Tax (assume 25%) ₹0.25 crore → **net profit ₹0.75 crore (7.5%)**.

If revenue grows 40% but COGS grows 60% (more discounts, costlier shipping), gross margin falls — exactly Aditya's problem.

steps.title: Questions to ask about any P&L
steps.body:
- What's the **gross margin** trend? (Pricing power and cost control.)
- Which **opex lines** are growing faster than revenue?
- Is EBITDA positive? Is the business **operationally profitable**?
- What's **one-off** vs recurring?
- How does this compare to **budget** and **last year**?

steps.title: Common confusions
steps.body:
- **Revenue ≠ profit.** Growth can destroy value if margins are negative.
- **EBITDA ≠ cash.** It ignores capital spending, working capital and interest.
- **Margin vs markup:** a product costing ₹60 sold at ₹100 has a 40% margin (40/100) but a 67% markup (40/60).

lessons.title: Balance sheet, cash flow and working capital

scenes.text: Sunita's auto-parts firm in Pune lands a big order from a car maker. The P&L shows a healthy profit.
But the customer pays in 90 days, while Sunita must pay suppliers in 30 and salaries every month.
By month two she can't pay suppliers. Her bank explains: 'Profit is an opinion; cash is a fact.'
She negotiates 60-day supplier terms and arranges a working-capital loan. The order becomes a success.

steps.title: The balance sheet
steps.body:
A **balance sheet** is a snapshot at a point in time:
**Assets = Liabilities + Equity**
- **Assets:** what the business owns or is owed — cash, receivables (money customers owe), inventory, machines, software.
- **Liabilities:** what it owes — payables to suppliers, loans, taxes due.
- **Equity:** owners' stake — capital invested plus retained profits.

It always balances because every rupee of assets is financed either by borrowing or by owners.

steps.title: Cash flow statement
steps.body:
Shows how cash moved in a period, in three parts:
- **Operating:** cash from running the business (profit adjusted for non-cash items and working-capital changes).
- **Investing:** buying/selling assets (machines, acquisitions).
- **Financing:** loans, repayments, equity raised, dividends.

A company can show profit and still run out of cash if customers pay slowly, inventory piles up, or big investments are made.

steps.title: Worked example: the cash conversion cycle
steps.body:
**Cash conversion cycle (CCC) = inventory days + receivable days − payable days.**
Sunita: inventory 30 days + receivables 90 days − payables 30 days = **90 days** her cash is tied up.
After negotiating supplier terms to 60 days: 30 + 90 − 60 = **60 days**.
Shorter CCC = less cash needed to grow. Levers: collect faster, hold less inventory, pay later (fairly — Indian MSME rules require timely payment to registered micro and small suppliers).

steps.title: Manager's takeaway
steps.body: Even if you don't work in finance, your decisions affect cash: payment terms you agree with customers, inventory you order, capital projects you request. Ask: *'When does the cash come in, and when does it go out?'*

scenes.text: Zoya opens a cloud kitchen in Bengaluru. Orders are booming on delivery apps.
Her mentor asks: 'After food cost, packaging, app commission and discounts, what do you earn per order?' Zoya doesn't know.
It's ₹18 per order. Her monthly fixed costs are ₹2.7 lakh. She needs 15,000 orders a month just to break even.
She cuts discounts, raises prices on bestsellers and adds high-margin combos. Contribution rises to ₹45 and break-even drops to 6,000 orders.

steps.title: Fixed vs variable costs; contribution
steps.body:
- **Variable costs** change with each unit sold (ingredients, packaging, commission, delivery).
- **Fixed costs** stay roughly the same regardless of volume within a range (rent, salaries, software).
- **Contribution per unit = price − variable cost per unit.**
- **Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ contribution per unit.**

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
Zoya (revised): average order ₹350; variable costs ₹305 (food ₹120, packaging ₹25, app commission ₹90, discount ₹40, other ₹30). Contribution = ₹45.
Fixed costs ₹2,70,000/month → **break-even = 2,70,000 ÷ 45 = 6,000 orders/month** (≈ 200 a day).

steps.title: Unit economics for subscription and tech businesses
steps.body:
- **CAC (customer acquisition cost)** = sales & marketing spend ÷ new customers.
- **LTV (lifetime value)** ≈ average monthly contribution per customer × expected customer lifetime (months).
- A common rule of thumb in SaaS is **LTV : CAC of about 3 : 1 or better**, and **CAC payback** within roughly a year — heuristics, not laws.
- **Churn** (customers leaving) dramatically affects LTV: if monthly churn is 5%, average lifetime ≈ 1 ÷ 0.05 = 20 months.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating discounts as marketing and forgetting they reduce contribution.
- Ignoring returns and cancellations (very significant in Indian e-commerce, including cash-on-delivery refusals).
- 'We'll make it up on volume' — if contribution is negative, more volume means bigger losses.

lessons.title: Building a business case: payback and NPV

scenes.text: Manish proposes ₹1.2 crore of sorting robots for a Gurugram warehouse. He says it 'will save a lot'.
The CFO asks: 'How much, when, and compared to what?'
Manish builds a business case: ₹40 lakh savings a year for 5 years, a payback of 3 years, and an NPV at 12%.
Approved — with a pilot milestone at month six.

steps.title: Structure of a business case
steps.body:
- **Problem / opportunity** (with numbers).
- **Options** (including do nothing).
- **Costs:** upfront (capex) and ongoing (opex).
- **Benefits:** savings, revenue, risk reduction — over time.
- **Financial metrics:** payback, NPV, sometimes IRR.
- **Risks and assumptions** — and sensitivity (what if savings are 30% lower?).
- **Recommendation and milestones.**

steps.title: Payback and time value of money
steps.body:
**Payback period** = how long until cumulative benefits equal the investment. Manish: ₹1.2 crore ÷ ₹40 lakh/year = **3 years**. Simple, but it ignores benefits after payback and the time value of money.

**Time value of money:** ₹100 today is worth more than ₹100 in a year (you could invest it). **Discounting** converts future cash to today's value: PV = CF ÷ (1 + r)^t, where r is the discount rate (often the company's cost of capital).

steps.title: Worked example: NPV
steps.body:
Investment ₹120 lakh today; savings ₹40 lakh/year for 5 years; discount rate 12%.
Present values: Year 1: 40/1.12 ≈ 35.7; Y2: 40/1.2544 ≈ 31.9; Y3: ≈ 28.5; Y4: ≈ 25.4; Y5: ≈ 22.7. Sum ≈ **144.2 lakh**.
**NPV = 144.2 − 120 ≈ +₹24 lakh** → positive, so it creates value at a 12% hurdle rate.
In Excel: =NPV(12%, savings range) − investment (note Excel's NPV assumes the first value is one period from now).

steps.title: Sensitivity analysis
steps.body: Test the key assumptions: if savings are only ₹30 lakh/year, PV ≈ 108 lakh → NPV ≈ −₹12 lakh. Now leadership knows **the case depends on achieving savings above roughly ₹33 lakh/year** — which is why a pilot milestone makes sense. Presenting sensitivity shows honesty and builds trust.

activity.label: Annual savings from the robots (₹ lakh), 5 years, 12% discount rate, ₹120 lakh investment

scenes.text: Rekha in a Kolkata FMCG firm copies a commission formula down 400 rows. The tax rate cell reference shifts with each row.
Half the commissions are calculated with blank cells as the rate. Payouts are wrong.
A colleague shows her the $ sign: $B$1 stays fixed when copied.
She also adds a check total. Errors like this are now caught before payouts.

steps.title: Core formulas
steps.body:
- **=SUM(B2:B100)**, **=AVERAGE()**, **=MIN()**, **=MAX()**, **=COUNT()** (numbers), **=COUNTA()** (non-empty).
- **=IF(C2>=100000,"Target met","Below")** — logic.
- **=ROUND(C2*0.18,2)** — rounding (e.g., GST at 18%).
- **=IFERROR(formula,0)** — handle errors gracefully (but don't hide real problems).
- **=TEXT(A2,"dd-mmm-yyyy")** — format dates as text.

steps.title: Relative vs absolute references
steps.body:
- **A1** (relative): changes when copied (A1 → A2 when copied down).
- **$A$1** (absolute): never changes.
- **$A1 / A$1** (mixed): locks column or row only.

Press **F4** (on Windows Excel) while editing a reference to cycle through these. Use absolute references for constants like tax rates, exchange rates, targets — and keep constants in clearly labelled cells, never typed inside formulas.

steps.title: Worked example: commission
steps.body:
B1 = commission rate (5%). Sales in C2:C401.
Commission in D2: **=C2*$B$1**, copied down. Check: **=SUM(D2:D401)** should equal **=SUM(C2:C401)*B1**. A quick check formula like this catches many errors.

steps.title: Spreadsheet risk
steps.body: Studies of real-world spreadsheets have repeatedly found errors are common. Protect yourself: label inputs, separate inputs/calculations/outputs, add check totals, avoid hard-coded numbers in formulas, and have someone review important models.

He starts doing it manually with Ctrl+F. It would take days.
A teammate writes one XLOOKUP formula and copies it down. Done in two minutes.
They also find 37 IDs that don't match — new joiners missing from the department list.

steps.title: XLOOKUP
steps.body:
Available in Microsoft 365 and Excel 2021 and later:
**=XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found])**
Example: **=XLOOKUP(A2, Depts!A:A, Depts!C:C, "Not found")** — finds A2's ID in column A of the Depts sheet and returns column C.

Advantages: looks left or right, exact match by default, built-in 'not found' value.

steps.title: INDEX/MATCH and VLOOKUP
steps.body:
For older versions:
- **=INDEX(Depts!C:C, MATCH(A2, Depts!A:A, 0))** — MATCH finds the row (0 = exact match), INDEX returns the value.
- **=VLOOKUP(A2, Depts!A:C, 3, FALSE)** — works only when the ID is the first column; **always use FALSE** (exact) for IDs, or you may get wrong matches silently.

steps.title: Why lookups fail
steps.body:
- Extra spaces: use **=TRIM()**.
- Numbers stored as text (e.g., '00123' vs 123): convert consistently.
- Duplicates in the lookup list: lookups return the first match only — check uniqueness.
- Approximate match accidentally on (VLOOKUP without FALSE).

steps.title: Pivot tables
steps.body:
Steps: select your data (ideally formatted as a Table with Ctrl+T), **Insert → PivotTable**, then drag fields:
- **Rows:** State
- **Columns:** Month (group dates by month)
- **Values:** Sum of Amount
- **Filters:** Product category

Refresh when data changes. Pivot tables summarise thousands of rows in seconds and let you slice data differently by dragging fields.

steps.title: SUMIFS and COUNTIFS
steps.body:
- **=SUMIFS(Amount, State, "Kerala", Month, "Jan")** — sum with multiple conditions.
- **=COUNTIFS(State, "Kerala", Amount, ">10000")** — count with conditions.
- **=AVERAGEIFS()** similarly.

Use them for fixed report layouts and to cross-check pivot results.

steps.title: Worked example: a cross-check

steps.title: Analyst habits
steps.body:
- Keep raw data untouched in one sheet; analyse in another.
- Use Tables so ranges expand automatically.
- Note data source and date on every report.
- Explain the 'so what': *'Kerala sales dropped 18% in January, mostly in the snacks category.'*

steps.title: Cleaning checklist
steps.body:
- **TRIM** spaces; **PROPER/UPPER** for consistent case.
- **Standardise** synonyms (Bombay → Mumbai, Bengaluru/Bangalore) with a mapping table.
- **Remove duplicates** (Data → Remove Duplicates) — but first define what counts as a duplicate (same email? same phone?).
- **Fix data types:** dates as dates, numbers as numbers.
- **Handle blanks:** decide whether to exclude, fill, or flag.
- **Validate:** totals and counts before vs after cleaning.

steps.title: A simple dashboard
steps.body:
- **3–5 key metrics** at the top (e.g., revenue, orders, average order value, return rate) with comparison to last period.
- **One trend chart** (line).
- **One breakdown** (sorted bar by region or product).
- **Filters/slicers** for period and region.
- **Notes:** data source, refresh date, definitions.

Design for the question the reader asks every week, not for every possible chart.

steps.title: Data privacy
steps.body: Customer data (names, phones, emails, addresses) is personal data. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 sets obligations for handling personal data, with rules being brought into force in phases — follow your company's data policies. Share only what's necessary, mask personal details in dashboards, and never email raw customer lists to personal accounts.

steps.title: Beyond Excel
steps.body: As data grows, teams move to tools like Power BI, Tableau, Looker or SQL databases, and Python for analysis. The thinking is the same: clean data, clear metric definitions, honest charts and a clear 'so what'.

lessons.title: Discovery: falling in love with the problem

scenes.text: A Bengaluru agri-tech startup builds a complex crop-price prediction feature for farmers. Usage after launch: 2%.
PM Kavitha visits farmers in Karnataka villages and listens.
Farmers say their real problem is knowing which nearby mandi pays the best price today — and how to get a truck there.
A simpler 'today's prices near you + transport booking' feature, with voice in Kannada, reaches 40% weekly usage.

steps.title: Problem before solution
steps.body:
A PM's first job is to understand **who** the user is, **what problem** they have, **how painful** it is, and **how they solve it today**. A common framing is **Jobs To Be Done (JTBD)**: *'When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [outcome].'*
Example: *'When my harvest is ready, I want to know which nearby mandi pays the most today, so I can earn more without wasting a trip.'*

steps.title: User interviews that work
steps.body:
- Ask about **past behaviour**, not hypothetical futures: *'Tell me about the last time you sold your crop.'* not *'Would you use an app that…?'*
- Ask **why** and **how** repeatedly; listen more than talk.
- Avoid leading questions (*'Don't you think this would be great?'*).
- Talk to **5–10 users** per segment to see patterns.
- Observe in context if possible — the field, the shop, the office.

steps.title: Worked example: validating cheaply
steps.body: Before building, Kavitha tested demand with a WhatsApp message at 7 am in three villages listing the top 5 mandi prices. In two weeks, 600 farmers had subscribed and asked for transport help. This **'concierge MVP'** (doing it manually first) proved demand before engineering spent months.

steps.title: Discovery traps
steps.body:
- Building what the loudest customer or the CEO asks for without understanding the underlying problem.
- Designing for 'users like me' (urban, English-speaking, high-end phone) when real users differ.
- Confusing **stated** preferences ('I'd pay for that') with **revealed** behaviour (do they actually pay?).

lessons.title: Prioritisation: RICE, MoSCoW and saying no

scenes.text: Rahul, PM at a Pune HR-tech company, has 50 feature requests from sales, support, the CEO and customers.
Everyone says theirs is urgent. Sales threatens a lost deal.
Rahul scores items with RICE and shares the scoring openly.
Stakeholders still argue, but now about numbers and assumptions, not volume. The roadmap gains trust.

steps.title: RICE scoring
steps.body:
**RICE = (Reach × Impact × Confidence) ÷ Effort** (a framework popularised by Intercom):
- **Reach:** users affected per period (e.g., 4,000/quarter).
- **Impact:** effect per user (e.g., 3 = massive, 2 = high, 1 = medium, 0.5 = low, 0.25 = minimal).
- **Confidence:** how sure you are (100%, 80%, 50%).
- **Effort:** person-months.

It forces explicit assumptions and makes comparison fairer.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body:
- **Bulk payroll upload:** Reach 2,000, Impact 2, Confidence 80%, Effort 2 → (2000×2×0.8)/2 = **1,600**.
- **Dark mode:** Reach 8,000, Impact 0.25, Confidence 100%, Effort 1 → **2,000**.
- **SSO for enterprise:** Reach 500, Impact 3, Confidence 80%, Effort 3 → **400**.

The scores are inputs to judgement, not the final answer — SSO may still be strategic if it unlocks big enterprise deals. Say so explicitly.

steps.title: Other tools
steps.body:
- **MoSCoW:** Must, Should, Could, Won't (this time) — good for release scope.
- **Kano model:** basic expectations vs performance features vs delighters.
- **Cost of delay:** how much value is lost per week of delay.
- **Impact vs effort 2×2:** quick wins, big bets, fill-ins, money pits.

steps.title: Saying no gracefully
steps.body:
*'Thanks — this is a real problem for those customers. It's not in this quarter's plan because we're focused on payroll accuracy, which affects 10× more users. I've logged it with your data; we'll revisit in the next planning cycle. Is there a workaround that would help in the meantime?'*
Acknowledge, explain the trade-off, record it, offer an alternative.

scenes.text: A PM writes a one-line ticket: 'Add referral programme.' Engineers build a share button.
Marketing expected rewards, tracking, fraud checks and UPI cashback.
The next PM, Sneha, writes a proper PRD with goals, user stories, scope, non-goals and metrics.
The referral launch works first time, with fraud rules preventing fake accounts.

steps.title: What a PRD contains
steps.body:
A **product requirements document** (or one-pager/spec):
- **Problem & why now** (with evidence).
- **Goals and success metrics.**
- **Users & use cases** (user stories: *'As a customer, I want to invite a friend so we both get ₹100 cashback'*).
- **Scope:** what's in; **non-goals:** what's out.
- **Requirements & acceptance criteria.**
- **Edge cases & risks** (fraud, privacy, accessibility, low-end phones, poor networks).
- **Open questions; launch plan.**

steps.title: Choosing metrics
steps.body:
- **North Star metric:** the one metric that best captures value delivered to users (e.g., weekly active merchants who received a payment).
- **AARRR funnel** (Dave McClure's 'pirate metrics'): Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue.
- **Guardrail metrics:** what must not get worse (crash rate, fraud, support tickets, page load time).
- Define metrics precisely: *'Activation = merchant receives first payment within 7 days of signup.'*

steps.title: Worked example: A/B test thinking
steps.body:
Hypothesis: *'Showing ₹100 cashback on the home screen will increase referrals sent by 20%.'*
- Control: current home screen. Variant: cashback banner.
- Primary metric: referrals sent per active user. Guardrail: fraud rate.
- Decide the sample size and run time *before* starting, and don't stop early just because results look good — that inflates false positives.

steps.title: Vanity metrics
steps.body: Downloads, page views or registered users can look impressive while real value is low. Prefer metrics tied to repeated value (active use, retention, completed transactions).

scenes.text: A shopping app launches a new checkout to 100% of users on the first day of the Diwali sale.
A bug with one bank's cards causes failed payments for hours, during peak traffic.
Next year, PM Arjun launches in stages: 1% → 10% → 50% → 100% over two weeks before the sale, with a kill switch.
Two bugs are found at 1% and fixed. Diwali checkout runs smoothly.

steps.title: Staged rollouts
steps.body:
- **Feature flags** let you turn features on for a percentage of users and off instantly.
- **Staged rollout:** internal users → 1% → 10% → 50% → 100%, watching metrics and guardrails at each stage.
- **Kill switch & rollback plan** ready before launch.
- **Avoid launching big changes right before peak events** unless they've been tested at scale.

steps.title: Go-to-market checklist
steps.body:
- **Support** trained with FAQs; **sales** briefed.
- **Docs and in-app guidance** ready (in relevant languages).
- **Marketing** messages aligned with what's actually shipping.
- **Legal/compliance** checks (privacy, payments rules, accessibility).
- **Monitoring dashboards** and on-call owners.

steps.title: After launch: learn
steps.body:
- Review metrics vs hypothesis at 1, 2 and 4 weeks.
- Read support tickets and user feedback.
- Decide: **iterate, scale, or roll back.**
- Write a short launch retro: what worked, what didn't, what we'll do differently.

A launch is the start of learning, not the end of the project.

steps.title: India-specific considerations
steps.body: Test on low-end Android phones and poor networks, support regional languages, consider UPI and cash-on-delivery flows, and remember festive peaks (Diwali, regional festivals, salary days around the 1st) bring huge traffic spikes.

lessons.title: Scope, WBS and the critical path

scenes.text: Farhan must move a 200-person Hyderabad office to a new building in 8 weeks. His plan is a single line: 'Move office'.
Week 3: nobody ordered network cabling, which takes 4 weeks to deliver.
A PMO colleague helps him break the work into a WBS and map dependencies.
They find the critical path runs through cabling and fit-out. Expedited ordering saves the deadline.

steps.title: The constraints
steps.body:
Every project balances **scope, time and cost** (the classic 'triple constraint'), with **quality**, risk and stakeholder satisfaction close behind. Change one and the others are affected: more scope with the same deadline needs more cost or carries more risk.

Start with a **project charter**: objective, scope, key deliverables, timeline, budget, sponsor, success criteria.

steps.title: Work breakdown structure (WBS)
steps.body:
Break the deliverable into smaller **work packages** until each can be estimated and owned:
- **Office move** → Site readiness (fit-out, cabling, furniture) · IT (network, desks, testing) · People (seating plan, communication) · Logistics (packing, movers) · Closure (old-site handover).

The WBS is about **deliverables**, not a to-do list in random order. Anything not in the WBS is not in scope.

steps.title: Worked example: critical path
steps.body:
Tasks (days): **A** design layout (3) → **B** order furniture (4) → **D** install & test (2); **A** → **C** network cabling (6) → **D**.
- Path A-B-D = 3 + 4 + 2 = **9 days**.
- Path A-C-D = 3 + 6 + 2 = **11 days**.

The **critical path** is the longest path: **A-C-D, 11 days**. Any delay on A, C or D delays the project. B has **float** (slack) of 2 days.

steps.title: Estimating
steps.body:
- Ask the people doing the work.
- Use ranges or three-point estimates: (Optimistic + 4×Most likely + Pessimistic) ÷ 6 (the PERT formula).
- Add contingency based on risk — and make it visible, not hidden padding.
- Track actual vs estimate to improve over time.

scenes.text: A Mumbai bank's CRM project reports 'green' for six months. Inside, it's red: data migration is far behind.
Two weeks before go-live, the truth comes out. Go-live slips four months.
New PM Anita introduces a risk register and honest RAG status with clear criteria.
Problems now surface early, and the sponsor trusts the reports.

steps.title: Risk register
steps.body:
For each risk: **description, probability, impact, owner, response, trigger.** Responses to threats:
- **Avoid** (change plan to remove it)
- **Mitigate** (reduce probability or impact)
- **Transfer** (insurance, contract)
- **Accept** (with contingency)
- **Escalate** (outside your authority)

A **risk** is uncertain and in the future; an **issue** has already happened.

steps.title: Stakeholder management
steps.body: Identify stakeholders, assess their **power and interest**, understand what they need, and plan communication: who gets what, how often, in what format. A **RACI** chart (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) clarifies roles — with exactly **one Accountable** per deliverable.

steps.title: Worked example: honest RAG status
steps.body:
Define criteria in advance:
- **Green:** on track for date, budget and scope.
- **Amber:** at risk; recovery plan within the team's control.
- **Red:** will miss without sponsor decision or help.

*'Status: AMBER. Data migration 2 weeks behind (62% vs 80% planned). Recovery: added 2 data engineers; will recover by 15 May. Decision needed: none yet; will escalate to Red if not recovered by 1 May.'*

steps.title: Watermelon reporting
steps.body: 'Green outside, red inside' happens when people fear bad news. Leaders get honest reports by **thanking people for early amber/red**, not punishing them. As a PM, report reality — your credibility is the project's most important asset.

scenes.text: A Chennai team says they 'do Scrum': 2-hour daily stand-ups, a manager assigning tasks, and sprints with no goal.
Developers hate it; delivery is no faster.
A new Scrum Master, Elena, walks them through the Scrum Guide's actual structure.
With a Sprint Goal, a 15-minute Daily Scrum and a real Product Owner, the team ships a usable increment every sprint.

steps.title: Scrum in one page (Scrum Guide 2020)
steps.body:
**Three accountabilities:** Product Owner (maximises product value; owns the Product Backlog), Scrum Master (establishes Scrum and helps the team improve), Developers (create the usable Increment each Sprint).

**Five events:** the **Sprint** (fixed length, one month or less), **Sprint Planning**, **Daily Scrum** (15 minutes, for the Developers), **Sprint Review**, **Sprint Retrospective**.

**Three artifacts, each with a commitment:** Product Backlog → **Product Goal**; Sprint Backlog → **Sprint Goal**; Increment → **Definition of Done**.

Scrum teams are typically **10 or fewer** people and are self-managing.

steps.title: Agile values
Common Scrum anti-patterns
steps.body:
- Daily Scrum as a long status meeting for a manager.
- No Sprint Goal — just a list of tickets.
- Product Owner is a committee or unavailable.
- 'Done' means 'coded' but not tested or deployable.
- Skipping retrospectives when busy (the time you need them most).
- Changing sprint scope constantly in ways that endanger the Sprint Goal.

steps.title: Certification note
steps.body: Scrum certifications are offered by different bodies (e.g., Scrum.org and Scrum Alliance), with their own formats. PMI's PMP exam covers predictive, agile and hybrid approaches and has eligibility requirements (project-management education hours and experience, depending on your education). *Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. lessons.title: Kanban flow and choosing an approach

story.title: The support team drowning in tickets

scenes.text: A Noida IT support team has 300 open tickets and everyone works on 8 at once.
Average resolution takes 9 days; customers are furious.
They adopt a Kanban board with WIP limits: no more than 3 tickets 'In progress' per person.
Within a month, resolution time drops to 4 days — by doing less at once.

steps.title: Kanban basics
steps.body:
- **Visualise** work on a board (To do → In progress → Review → Done).
- **Limit work in progress (WIP)** per column or person.
- **Manage flow:** measure cycle time and throughput; remove bottlenecks.
- **Make policies explicit** (what 'done' means for each column).
- **Improve continuously.**

Kanban suits continuous work (support, operations, maintenance) where fixed sprints feel artificial.

steps.title: Little's Law
steps.body:
For a stable system: **average cycle time = average WIP ÷ average throughput.**
If a team has 60 items in progress and completes 15 per week, average cycle time ≈ 60 ÷ 15 = **4 weeks**. Halve WIP to 30 with the same throughput → about **2 weeks**. This is why WIP limits speed things up.

steps.title: Predictive, agile or hybrid?
steps.body:
- **Predictive (waterfall):** clear, stable requirements; high cost of change (construction, regulatory projects, hardware).
- **Agile (Scrum/Kanban):** uncertain requirements, need for fast feedback (software products, digital services).
- **Hybrid:** common in large enterprises — e.g., fixed milestones and budgets with agile delivery inside.

Choose based on uncertainty and cost of change, not fashion.

steps.title: Stop starting, start finishing
steps.body: The Kanban slogan captures the lesson: finishing work delivers value; starting work only creates inventory. When you're tempted to pick a new ticket, first ask: *'Can I help finish something already in progress?'*

story.title: The vendor who knew his walk-away

scenes.text: Procurement manager Deepika negotiates a ₹2 crore annual facilities contract in Mumbai. The vendor asks for ₹2.4 crore.
She has prepared: a second vendor quote at ₹2.1 crore (her BATNA) and market benchmarks.
She anchors at ₹1.9 crore with a clear rationale. The vendor's own walk-away is around ₹2.0 crore.
They settle at ₹2.05 crore with better service levels. Both sides feel it's fair.

steps.title: Key concepts
steps.body:
From *Getting to Yes* (Fisher & Ury) and negotiation research:
- **BATNA:** Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement — what you'll do if there's no deal. A strong BATNA is your biggest source of power.
- **Reservation point (walk-away):** the worst deal you'll accept.
- **ZOPA:** Zone Of Possible Agreement — the overlap between both sides' reservation points.
- **Anchoring:** the first number often strongly influences the outcome.

steps.title: Worked example: finding the ZOPA
steps.body:
Buyer (Deepika): walk-away = ₹2.1 crore (her BATNA quote). Seller: walk-away = ₹2.0 crore (below this he'd lose money).
**ZOPA = ₹2.0 – 2.1 crore.** A deal anywhere in this range beats both sides' alternatives. If the seller's walk-away were ₹2.2 crore, there would be **no ZOPA** — and walking away would be rational.

steps.title: Using anchors well
steps.body:
- If you have good information, **anchor first** — ambitious but justifiable (*'Based on two benchmarks, we're looking at ₹1.9 crore'*).
- If the other side anchors extremely, **don't counter immediately**; re-anchor with your own rationale.
- Always attach a **reason** to numbers.
- Prepare a list of **tradeables**: payment terms, volume, contract length, service levels, delivery dates.

steps.title: Preparation mistakes
steps.body:
- Not knowing your BATNA — you'll accept bad deals or reject good ones.
- Revealing your walk-away.
- Negotiating only on price.
- Bluffing about alternatives you don't have — it can backfire and damages trust.

scenes.text: A startup founder, Kiran, and an enterprise client in Dubai are stuck on price: he wants ₹80 lakh, they offer ₹60 lakh.
Kiran asks why ₹60 lakh. The client's budget for this financial year is capped; next year's budget is larger.
He proposes ₹60 lakh this year for phase 1, with phase 2 at ₹35 lakh next year, plus a case-study right.
Both get more than their original positions.

steps.title: Positions vs interests
steps.body:
A **position** is what someone says they want (*'₹60 lakh max'*). An **interest** is why (*budget cap this year, need to show results to leadership*). Solving for interests creates options: phasing, payment terms, scope, guarantees, references.

Ask: *'Help me understand what's driving that number?'* and *'What would make this work for you?'*

steps.title: Trading concessions
steps.body:
- **Never give without getting:** *'If you can commit to a 3-year term, we can reduce the annual fee by 5%.'*
- **Concede in decreasing steps** (e.g., 5%, then 2%, then 1%) — it signals you're nearing your limit.
- **Trade low-cost-to-you, high-value-to-them** items.
- **Package** issues together rather than settling one at a time.

steps.title: Recognising tough tactics
steps.body:
- **Good cop/bad cop** — address the decision-maker's interests directly.
- **Last-minute nibble** ('just add free training') — trade: *'Sure, if we can finalise today.'*
- **Fake deadline / exploding offer** — test it calmly.
- **Silence** — don't rush to fill it with concessions.
- **Personal attacks** — name it calmly and refocus on the issues.

Use ethical tactics yourself: lying about material facts can harm relationships and, in some cases, have legal consequences.

steps.title: Cultural notes
steps.body: In many Indian business settings, negotiation is relationship-based and bargaining is expected — a first offer is rarely final. With some global counterparts (e.g., in parts of Northern Europe), first offers may be closer to final and heavy haggling can seem untrustworthy. Research the counterpart's norms and adapt.

lessons.title: Discovery selling: questions that uncover needs

scenes.text: Sales rep Arnav opens his meeting with a Delhi hospital chain by demoing all 40 features of his software.
The CIO checks her phone. 'Thanks, we'll get back to you.' They never do.
His manager coaches him to ask questions first: what's happening now, what's the problem, what it costs, what a solution would be worth.
At the next hospital, the CIO reveals that billing errors cost them crores a year. Arnav demos only the three features that solve it. Deal won.

steps.title: SPIN questions
steps.body:
From Neil Rackham's research on large sales (*SPIN Selling*):
- **Situation:** facts about the current state (*'How do you handle billing today?'*). Use sparingly.
- **Problem:** difficulties (*'Where do errors happen?'*).
- **Implication:** consequences (*'What does that cost in rework and delayed insurance claims?'*).
- **Need-payoff:** value of solving it (*'If errors fell by half, what would that mean for your team?'*).

Implication and need-payoff questions help the buyer articulate value themselves.

steps.title: Qualification
steps.body:
Not every lead is worth pursuing. Frameworks help:
- **BANT:** Budget, Authority, Need, Timeline.
- **MEDDIC:** Metrics, Economic buyer, Decision criteria, Decision process, Identify pain, Champion.

Ask respectfully: *'Who else is involved in the decision? What does your approval process look like? Is there a budget set aside?'*

steps.title: Worked example: discovery flow
steps.body:
- S: *'How many claims do you submit monthly?'* → 12,000.
- P: *'What share get rejected first time?'* → about 9%.
- I: *'What happens to a rejected claim?'* → 2–3 weeks delay, staff time, cash-flow strain.
- N: *'If first-time rejection fell to 3%, what would that free up?'* → *'Probably two people's time and faster cash.'*
Now the demo focuses on claims validation — and the value is in the client's own words.

steps.title: Listen more than talk
steps.body: Many sales coaches advise letting the customer talk for most of a discovery call. Take notes, summarise back (*'So the biggest issue is first-time claim rejection, costing roughly…'*), and confirm before proposing.

scenes.text: A Coimbatore textile firm tells salesperson Meghna, 'Your ERP is too expensive.'
Instead of discounting, she asks, 'Expensive compared to what?'
They're comparing with a cheaper tool that lacks GST e-invoicing integration they need. She shows the cost of manual work.
They sign — and a year later expand to three more plants because the implementation went well.

steps.title: Handling objections
steps.body:
A simple sequence:
- **Listen** fully.
- **Acknowledge** (*'That's a fair concern.'*).
- **Explore** (*'Compared to what? What would make it worth it?'*).
- **Respond** with evidence (ROI, references, trial, guarantees).
- **Confirm** (*'Does that address it?'*).

Common objections: price, timing ('not now'), status quo ('we're fine'), risk ('what if it fails?'), authority ('I need approval').

steps.title: Closing ethically
steps.body:
- **Summarise value and agreed next steps.**
- **Ask directly:** *'Shall we go ahead with the pilot starting 1 March?'*
- Use a **mutual action plan**: dates for legal review, security review, signature, kick-off.
- Avoid pressure tactics and false scarcity. Never promise features that don't exist or misrepresent terms — it damages trust and can create legal exposure.

steps.title: Account management
Ethics and compliance
steps.body: Gifts, hospitality and payments to win business are governed by company policy and anti-bribery laws (including India's Prevention of Corruption Act and, for many multinationals, laws like the US FCPA and UK Bribery Act). Dealing with government buyers has strict rules. When in doubt, ask compliance.

story.title: Anjali's first month as a Director

scenes.text: Anjali, a star engineering manager at a Hyderabad tech campus, is promoted to Director of 4 managers and 38 engineers.
She keeps doing what made her successful: reviewing code, joining every stand-up, solving technical problems herself.
Within six weeks, her managers feel micromanaged, two strategic projects are drifting, and she's working 14-hour days.
Her VP tells her: 'Your product is no longer the software. Your product is the team of teams.'

steps.title: From doing to designing
steps.body:
Leadership roles shift at each level (a well-known framing is the 'leadership pipeline'):
- **Individual contributor:** results through your own work.
- **First-line manager:** results through people — hiring, feedback, prioritising.
- **Manager of managers:** results through **managers** — choosing and developing leaders, setting direction across teams, allocating resources, designing structure and processes.

The skills that got you promoted (deep technical problem-solving, being the hero) can now hurt if overused. Your new leverage comes from **clarity, people decisions and systems**.

steps.title: Where your time should go
steps.body:
A useful self-audit: track your calendar for two weeks and sort time into:
- **Direction:** strategy, priorities, roadmap, cross-team alignment.
- **People:** 1:1s with managers, skip-levels, hiring, talent reviews, coaching.
- **Operations:** reviews, metrics, incidents, budgets.
- **Doing:** your own hands-on work.

Many new directors find 'doing' far too high and 'direction' and 'people' too low. There's no perfect ratio, but if you are the bottleneck for decisions inside a team, that's a signal.

steps.title: Classic traps
steps.body:
- **Skipping the manager:** giving direct instructions to their engineers. It undermines the manager's authority.
- **Being the escalation point for everything.** Push decisions down.
- **Measuring yourself by activity.** Your output = the output of your organisation.
- **Not letting go of your old team.** Treat your former peers and old team fairly and equally.

steps.title: Your first 90 days as a manager of managers
steps.body:
- 1:1 with each manager: their goals, team health, biggest risks, what they need from you.
- Skip-levels with a sample of engineers.
- Meet key peers and stakeholders (product, design, operations).
- Write a short **'state of the org'**: strengths, risks, 3 priorities — share it and invite corrections.
- Make one or two visible improvements; avoid large reorganisations before you understand the system.

activity.prompt: For a manager of managers, is this high-leverage or a trap?

Rewriting an engineer's code yourself at midnight
Clarifying priorities across four teams

scenes.text: Paul, a director in Bengaluru, hears from his managers that 'everything's fine'. Attrition, however, is 25% in one team.
He starts monthly skip-level conversations with small groups of engineers.
He learns that one manager cancels 1:1s, overloads on-call duty onto two people and takes credit in reviews.
Instead of overruling the manager publicly, Paul coaches him with specific feedback — and checks progress through the next skip-levels.

steps.title: Purpose of a skip-level
Worked example: good questions
steps.body:
- *'What's one thing slowing you down that leadership could fix?'*
- *'Do you understand why we're prioritising X over Y this quarter?'*
- *'What should I start, stop or continue?'*
- *'Who on the team has helped you most recently?'* (surfaces quiet heroes)
- *'How sustainable is your workload, 1–10?'*

In hierarchical cultures, people may hold back with a director. Use small groups, anonymous pre-surveys, and act visibly on what you hear so trust grows.

steps.title: Rules that protect your managers
steps.body:
- Tell managers you run skip-levels and why; share themes (not who said what).
- Don't make decisions in the skip-level that belong to the manager — take issues back to them.
- If you hear about a serious problem (harassment, ethics, safety), follow policy immediately — those don't wait.
- Close the loop: *'Last month you raised on-call load; here's what changed.'*

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using skip-levels to collect gossip.
- Breaking confidentiality ('Ravi said you're disorganised').
- Promising things the manager hasn't agreed to.
- Doing them once and never again — trust needs consistency.

a.text: In a skip-level, three engineers say their manager often cancels 1:1s and gives all weekend on-call to the same two people. What do you do?

choices.label: Thank them, promise to look into themes, and take it to the manager as coaching with specifics but without names
choices.feedback: Protects confidentiality and the manager's role.

choices.label: Immediately email the manager: 'Your team says you're bad at 1:1s.'
choices.feedback: Breaks trust on both sides.

choices.label: Reassign on-call yourself the same day
choices.feedback: Bypassing the manager undermines them.

b.text: The manager is defensive: 'They're exaggerating.' How do you respond?

choices.label: Share the observable data (1:1 cancellations, on-call rota) and agree a plan with a check-in date
choices.feedback: Data depersonalises and enables change.

choices.label: Drop it to avoid conflict
choices.feedback: The problem and attrition continue.

c.text: The manager is furious and starts asking who complained. What now?

choices.label: Apologise for the approach, make clear retaliation is unacceptable, reset with data-based coaching
choices.feedback: Recover, and protect the team.

d.text: The manager feels humiliated and the team is confused about who's in charge. What now?

choices.label: Talk with the manager, explain the concern, and let them own the fix
choices.feedback: Return authority to the manager.

e1.text: The manager fixes the rota and protects 1:1s. Next quarter's skip-level shows better morale and the attrition trend eases.

e2.text: Two more engineers resign. Avoiding hard coaching conversations is costly.
