options: Small groups, anonymous pre-surveys and visible follow-through

story.title: The migration Vikram couldn't let go

scenes.text: Senior Director Vikram 'delegates' a cloud migration to his manager Farah — then reviews every ticket and changes her plans.
Farah feels she has responsibility without authority. Her team waits for Vikram's approval on everything.
A coach introduces delegation levels and asks Vikram to define the outcome, constraints and check-ins — then step back.
The migration finishes early. Farah is promoted the following year.

steps.title: Levels of delegation
steps.body:
Make the level explicit:
- **1. Do as I say.**
- **2. Research and report; I decide.**
- **3. Recommend; I decide.**
- **4. Decide, then tell me.**
- **5. Decide; tell me only if there's a problem.**

For experienced managers on familiar work, aim for 4–5. For new or high-risk work, start at 3 and move up as trust grows. Many delegation failures come from the leader assuming level 5 and acting like level 1.

steps.title: Worked example: a delegation brief
steps.body:
*'Farah, I'd like you to own the migration to the new cloud region.*
- *Outcome: all payment services migrated by 30 Sept with no customer-visible downtime above 5 minutes.*
- *Constraints: budget ₹2.4 crore; no changes to the card-processing vendor.*
- *Authority: you decide sequencing, staffing within your teams and vendors under ₹25 lakh (level 4).*
- *Check-ins: fortnightly 30-minute review; escalate immediately if downtime risk exceeds the target.*
- *Support from me: unblocking with security and finance.'*

steps.title: Inspect, don't interfere
steps.body: Agree on **leading indicators** (milestones, risk register, test coverage) and review them at check-ins. Ask questions (*'What could stop us hitting 30 Sept?'*) instead of issuing instructions. Intervene only when risk crosses the agreed threshold — and say why.

steps.title: Reverse delegation
steps.body: Watch for 'monkeys on your back': a manager brings you a problem and leaves with you owning it. Reply with: *'What do you recommend?'* and *'What do you need from me to do it?'* — so ownership stays with them.

lessons.title: Coaching managers and building the bench

scenes.text: Meenakshi, a VP in Chennai, is offered a two-year global assignment. Her boss asks: 'Who can step into your role?'
She realises nobody is ready — she has always solved the hardest problems herself.
She spends six months coaching two directors: giving them her steering meetings, stretch projects and honest feedback.
One of them succeeds her. Meenakshi takes the assignment without the organisation wobbling.

steps.title: Coach with questions
steps.body:
A simple coaching structure is **GROW**:
- **Goal:** *What do you want to achieve?*
- **Reality:** *What's happening now? What have you tried?*
- **Options:** *What could you do? What else?*
- **Will / Way forward:** *What will you do, by when? What support do you need?*

Coaching builds judgement; telling builds dependence. Tell when it's urgent or the person truly lacks information; coach when they can find the answer.

steps.title: Succession and the bench
steps.body:
For each critical role (including yours), identify:
- **Ready now** successors,
- **Ready in 1–2 years,**
- the **gaps** for each (e.g., executive communication, P&L ownership, cross-functional influence),
- a **development plan**: stretch assignments, rotations, mentoring, exposure to senior forums.

Around 70% of development is often attributed to on-the-job experience (the '70-20-10' heuristic: experience, relationships, formal learning) — treat it as a rough guide, not a law.

steps.title: Worked example: a stretch assignment
steps.body: Meenakshi gave Director Arun her monthly business review with the CFO for three months. Before each, they rehearsed for 20 minutes; after each, she gave two points of feedback. By month three Arun ran it alone. Cost to her: about 2 hours a month. Benefit: a successor and a freed-up VP.

steps.title: Make the bench diverse and fair
steps.body: Bias easily creeps into who gets 'potential' labels — people who resemble current leaders, speak loudly, or are most visible. Use clear criteria, look at under-represented groups (including women returning from maternity or caregiving breaks), and ask: *who hasn't been given a stretch chance yet?*

courses.title: Strategy, OKRs, org design and influence
courses.summary: Turn ambiguity into a clear strategy, cascade it with OKRs, design organisations that fit the strategy, and influence peers and executives without formal authority.

story.title: 'Be the best' is not a strategy

scenes.text: At an offsite in Goa, a VP presents the 'strategy': 'Be the #1 payments platform in India, delight customers, grow 50%.'
A new director, Omar, asks: 'What will we stop doing? Where will we not compete?' Silence.
Over two days they diagnose: they can't beat incumbents in big-city retail, but small-town merchants are underserved.
New strategy: focus on Tier-2/3 merchants with vernacular onboarding and offline support; pause enterprise sales. Teams finally know what to say no to.

steps.title: Strategy = diagnosis + guiding policy + coherent actions
steps.body:
Richard Rumelt (*Good Strategy Bad Strategy*) describes the kernel of strategy:
- **Diagnosis:** what's really going on? What's the critical challenge?
- **Guiding policy:** the overall approach to deal with it — including what you *won't* do.
- **Coherent actions:** coordinated steps that carry out the policy.

**Bad strategy** signs: fluffy slogans, a list of goals with no approach ('grow 50%'), ignoring the main obstacle, or trying to do everything.

steps.title: Where to play, how to win
steps.body:
Another widely used framing (Lafley & Martin, *Playing to Win*) asks a cascade of choices: winning aspiration → **where to play** (segments, geographies, channels) → **how to win** (cost, differentiation, experience) → capabilities needed → management systems.

The key word is **choice**. A strategy that doesn't exclude anything isn't a strategy.

steps.title: Worked example: a one-page strategy
steps.body:
- **Diagnosis:** Big-city retail is saturated; incumbents have scale. Tier-2/3 merchants (≈ our fastest-growing signups) churn because onboarding is English-only and support is phone-unavailable.
- **Guiding policy:** Win small-town merchants through vernacular, assisted onboarding; deprioritise large enterprise deals for 18 months.
- **Coherent actions:** onboarding in 8 Indian languages; 500 field agents in 40 cities; partner with distributors; move 2 enterprise teams to merchant success.
- **Will not do:** custom enterprise integrations; new countries.

steps.title: Test your strategy
steps.body: Ask: *Does it name the critical challenge? Does it say what we won't do? Do the actions reinforce each other? Could a competitor copy it easily? Would a frontline employee know how to decide differently because of it?*

scenes.text: A Gurugram SaaS company adopts OKRs. Each team writes 8 objectives and 5 key results each, mostly tasks like 'launch feature X'.
By mid-quarter nobody remembers them. Bonuses are tied to scores, so everyone sandbagged.
The COO resets: 3 company objectives, measurable outcomes, no direct link to bonus, weekly check-ins.
Next quarter, activation rises and teams talk about outcomes, not output.

steps.title: OKR basics
steps.body:
**OKRs (Objectives and Key Results)** were developed at Intel under Andy Grove and popularised by John Doerr.
- **Objective:** qualitative, inspiring, time-bound direction. *'Make onboarding effortless for small merchants.'*
- **Key results (2–5):** measurable **outcomes** that show the objective is achieved. *'Activation within 7 days from 32% to 50%'*, *'Onboarding support tickets per 100 signups from 18 to 8'*.
- **Initiatives:** the projects you'll try (*'vernacular onboarding'*) — not the KRs themselves.

steps.title: Worked example: output vs outcome
steps.body:
- Output KR (weak): *'Launch Hindi onboarding.'*
- Outcome KR (strong): *'Hindi-speaking merchant activation from 25% to 45%.'*

If you can tick a KR without changing anything for customers, it's probably a task. Outcome KRs let teams choose better initiatives if the first idea fails.

steps.title: Common OKR failures
steps.body:
- **Too many** — aim for a few objectives per team.
- **Tasks disguised as KRs.**
- **Tying OKR scores directly to pay** — encourages sandbagging; many practitioners separate OKRs from compensation.
- **Set and forget** — no weekly or fortnightly check-ins.
- **Pure top-down cascade** — teams should propose OKRs that connect to company objectives, not just receive them.
- Ignoring **health metrics** (quality, reliability, attrition) while chasing growth.

steps.title: Committed vs aspirational
steps.body: Some organisations label KRs as **committed** (must hit ~100%) or **aspirational/moonshot** (achieving ~60–70% may be a good result). Make the type explicit so a 70% isn't misread as failure — or as success.

options: Be a good result if labelled aspirational

scenes.text: A Bengaluru e-commerce company reorganises from functional teams to product 'pods' — its third reorg in two years.
Six months later, the same problems remain: unclear decisions, slow releases. People are tired of reorgs.
A new CTO analyses: the problem wasn't the boxes; it was shared services with no clear owners and decisions needing six approvals.
She keeps the structure, clarifies decision rights and interfaces, and reduces approvals — releases speed up without another reorg.

steps.title: Common structures and trade-offs
steps.body:
- **Functional** (engineering, design, marketing): deep expertise, efficient; but slow cross-functional work.
- **Product/divisional** (teams per product or customer segment): fast, accountable; but duplication and weaker specialist depth.
- **Matrix** (reporting to both function and product): balances both; but dual bosses can cause conflict and slow decisions.
- **Platform + stream-aligned teams** (a pattern from *Team Topologies*): stream teams deliver to customers; platform teams provide self-service internal capabilities.

No structure is perfect. Choose what best supports the strategy, then manage its weaknesses.

steps.title: Beyond boxes: the other design levers
steps.body:
Structure is only one lever. Also design:
- **Decision rights:** who decides what (RACI, RAPID).
- **Interfaces:** how teams hand work to each other (APIs, SLAs, shared roadmaps).
- **Processes & cadence:** planning, reviews, budgeting.
- **Metrics & incentives.**
- **Talent & roles.**

If the real problem is unclear decision rights, a new org chart won't fix it.

steps.title: Worked example: spans and layers
steps.body: A **span of control** is the number of direct reports; **layers** are levels between CEO and frontline. Very narrow spans (e.g., 2–3 reports per manager) add layers, slow communication and raise cost; very wide spans can overload managers. Many tech organisations aim for roughly 6–10 reports per first-line manager, adjusted for work complexity and manager experience — use it as a starting heuristic, not a rule.

steps.title: Reorg hygiene
steps.body:
- Diagnose before redesigning; write the problem statement.
- Involve key leaders; test designs against real scenarios ('who decides X?').
- Communicate the *why*, not just the new chart.
- Move quickly once decided — prolonged uncertainty hurts morale.
- Respect people: role changes affect careers; handle with care and in line with HR policy and law.
- Avoid frequent reorgs; each one has a productivity cost.

scenes.text: Rashmi, a product director in Pune, needs the central security team to prioritise a review — or her launch slips a quarter. She has no authority over them.
Her first email, 'This is urgent and approved by my VP', gets a polite 'We'll add it to the queue.'
She meets the security lead, Gautam, asks about his goals, and learns his team is measured on reducing critical vulnerabilities.
She offers her engineers to fix two known vulnerabilities in exchange for an early review slot. Gautam agrees happily.

steps.title: Influence = understanding their currencies
steps.body:
Cohen and Bradford's *Influence Without Authority* describes influence as **exchange**: find what the other side values ('currencies') and offer it.
- **Task currencies:** resources, help, information.
- **Position currencies:** visibility, recognition, reputation.
- **Relationship currencies:** understanding, support, belonging.
- **Personal currencies:** gratitude, ownership, learning.
- **Inspiration currencies:** a meaningful mission.

Start by asking about *their* goals and pressures before making your ask.

steps.title: Cialdini's principles (use ethically)
steps.body: Robert Cialdini identified widely used principles of persuasion: **reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity** (later adding **unity**). Ethical use: genuine help (reciprocity), credible data and expertise (authority), real examples of peers (social proof). Manipulative use — fake urgency, false scarcity — destroys trust in organisations where you'll work with the same people for years.

steps.title: Worked example: pre-wiring a decision
Build the bank before you withdraw
steps.body: Invest in relationships when you *don't* need anything: share useful information, praise peers' teams publicly, help with their priorities. When you need a favour, you're drawing on trust you've built. And when someone says no, ask *'What would make this possible?'* — then go back with that.

courses.title: Hiring, calibration, firing and executive presence
courses.summary: Make the hardest people decisions well: structured hiring, fair performance calibration, performance improvement and exits handled with dignity, and the executive presence that makes people trust your judgement.

scenes.text: A Chennai team hires Karan after interviews where everyone 'had a great feeling'. He went to the same college as the hiring manager.
Six months later, Karan struggles with the core skill the role needed — system design — which no interviewer had tested properly.
The director introduces structured interviews: defined competencies, standard questions, scoring rubrics and independent written feedback before debrief.
Hiring quality improves, and the team becomes noticeably more diverse.

steps.title: Why structure beats gut feel
steps.body: Research on hiring consistently finds that **structured interviews** (same job-related questions, scored against defined criteria) predict job performance better than unstructured chats. Unstructured interviews are vulnerable to **affinity bias** (liking people like us), halo effects and first impressions.

steps.title: Designing the loop
steps.body:
- **Define the role:** 4–6 competencies that matter (e.g., system design, coding, stakeholder management, ownership).
- **Assign each interviewer** specific competencies — avoid everyone asking the same thing.
- **Use work samples** where possible (realistic tasks, case studies).
- **Behavioural questions** for past behaviour: *'Tell me about a time you had to deliver with unclear requirements.'*
- **Rubrics:** what does a 1, 3 and 5 answer look like?
- **Independent written feedback** before the debrief, to avoid groupthink.
- **Bar-raiser or independent interviewer** (used at some big tech firms) to protect standards.

steps.title: Worked example: a rubric
steps.body:
Competency: **Ownership**. Question: *'Tell me about a project that went wrong. What did you do?'*
- **1:** Blames others; no personal actions.
- **3:** Describes own actions to fix the immediate problem.
- **5:** Owns the outcome, fixes the problem, prevents recurrence, communicates proactively with stakeholders — with specific evidence.

Interviewers score with examples from the answer, not adjectives.

steps.title: Fairness and law
steps.body: Avoid questions about marital status, pregnancy or family plans, religion, caste, age, or health unrelated to job requirements — they invite bias and, in many jurisdictions, legal risk. Ensure diverse interview panels, consistent processes for all candidates, and respectful candidate experience (timely updates, no ghosting). Follow your company's HR and legal guidance.

scenes.text: In a calibration meeting, Manager Rohan passionately argues all his people deserve top ratings. Quieter manager Swathi presents data but gets interrupted.
Rohan's team ends up with most of the top ratings; Swathi's strong performers are pushed down.
The VP reviews outcomes and notices the pattern — and that women and remote workers were disproportionately rated lower.
Next cycle: pre-written evidence packets, a facilitator, bias checks and timeboxes per person.

steps.title: Purpose of calibration
steps.body: Calibration aligns rating standards across managers so that 'Exceeds' means the same in every team. Done well, it reduces individual manager bias. Done badly, it rewards the most persuasive managers.

steps.title: Running it well
steps.body:
- **Evidence packets** prepared in advance: goals, outcomes, examples, peer input.
- **Clear rating definitions** with examples.
- **Facilitator** (often HR or a neutral leader) to keep time and fairness.
- **Discuss the edges** (top and bottom) and cases where managers disagree.
- **Bias checks:** look at distributions by team, gender, location (remote vs office), tenure, part-time status, and people who took leave (e.g., parental leave).
- **Document decisions and reasons.**

steps.title: Common biases in ratings
steps.body:
- **Recency:** last month dominates.
- **Halo/horns:** one strong trait colours everything.
- **Proximity:** office-based people seen more.
- **Similarity/affinity.**
- **Leniency/central tendency:** everyone gets the middle or top.
- **'Potential' vs 'performance' confusion.**

Ask in the room: *'What's the evidence? Would we rate this the same if the person were in a different team or location?'*

steps.title: After calibration
steps.body: Managers must explain final ratings to employees honestly, focused on evidence and next steps — never 'HR forced me' (it shifts blame and undermines trust in the process). Where a rating went down in calibration, the manager should understand why and own the message.

statements.s: Calibration aims to make rating standards consistent across teams.
statements.why: That's its core purpose.

statements.s: The most passionate manager's view should carry the most weight.
statements.why: Evidence, not volume, should decide.

statements.s: Checking rating distributions by gender and location helps detect bias.
statements.why: Patterns can reveal systematic bias.

statements.why: Managers should own and explain the decision.

statements.s: Recency bias means overweighting recent events.
statements.why: Counter it with year-round evidence.

lessons.title: Underperformance, PIPs and exits with dignity

scenes.text: Manager Nisha has known for six months that one engineer, Ajay, isn't meeting the bar. She gives vague feedback and 'Meets' ratings to avoid conflict.
The team carries his work and becomes resentful. When Nisha finally starts a PIP, Ajay is shocked: 'You never told me.'
HR advises: clear documented feedback, a fair plan with support, and honest conversations.
Ajay doesn't meet the plan; he leaves with a respectful conversation and transition support. Nisha learns: kindness is clarity, early.

steps.title: Diagnose before you act
steps.body: Underperformance has causes: **unclear expectations, skill gaps, wrong role fit, personal circumstances (health, family), lack of resources, or motivation/conduct issues.** Ask before assuming: *'I've noticed X; what's getting in the way?'* Many problems are fixed with clarity, coaching or adjustments. Health and personal issues may need HR support, flexibility or EAP referral.

steps.title: Clear feedback and a fair improvement plan
steps.body:
- Give **specific, early, documented** feedback (SBI: situation, behaviour, impact).
- If needed, a **performance improvement plan (PIP)** should state: specific gaps, measurable expectations, support offered (training, mentoring, check-ins), timeline, and consequences.
- A PIP should be a **genuine chance to improve**, not a disguised exit paperwork exercise. Hold regular, documented check-ins.
- Involve HR early and follow company policy and applicable employment law.

steps.title: Exits and layoffs with dignity
steps.body:
Whether it's a performance exit or a layoff:
- Have the conversation **in private**, live (video or in person), not by email or by revoking access first without warning where avoidable.
- Be **clear and brief** about the decision; don't debate it or give false hope.
- Explain what happens next: last day, settlement, benefits, references, transition support.
- Allow emotion; listen.
- Tell the remaining team appropriately, without disparaging the person.

In India, termination procedures depend on the employment contract, company policy, and labour laws (India's four Labour Codes, notified in force from 21 November 2025, consolidate many older laws; rules continue to be phased in). Always work with HR and legal. *This is general education, not legal advice.*

steps.title: Avoid
steps.body:
- Years of inflated ratings, then a sudden exit (unfair and legally risky).
- Public discussion of someone's performance.
- Forcing resignations through humiliation or pressure.
- Firing someone soon after they raised a complaint without clear, documented, unrelated performance reasons — this can look like retaliation.

scenes.text: Two directors present budget requests to the CEO in Singapore. Raj speaks for 20 minutes, defensive under questions.
Lina states her ask in one sentence, gives three reasons, and says 'I don't know — I'll find out by Thursday' to one question.
When the CEO challenges her, she pauses and says, 'That's a fair concern. Here's what would change my mind.'
Lina gets her budget. Raj gets 'come back with a clearer case'.

steps.title: Presence = substance × communication × composure
steps.body:
'Executive presence' is often misread as looks, accent or confidence. In practice, senior leaders trust people who show:
- **Substance:** clear judgement, command of the facts, a point of view.
- **Communication:** concise, structured, audience-aware; answer first.
- **Composure:** calm under pressure, open to challenge, no defensiveness.

None of these depend on an accent, gender or 'fitting the mould' — they're learnable skills.

steps.title: Worked example: answering an executive
steps.body:
Question: *'Why should we invest ₹10 crore in this?'*

**Weak:** a 4-minute history of the project.

**Strong:** *'Because it reduces payment failures by a third, which we estimate is worth ₹25–30 crore a year. Three reasons we're confident: the Indore pilot data, vendor benchmarks, and customer interviews. The main risk is integration time; we've got a rollback plan.'* — 25 seconds, then stop and let them ask.

steps.title: Composure under challenge
steps.body:
- Pause before answering.
- Acknowledge: *'That's a fair concern.'*
- Separate what you know, what you believe and what you don't know.
- Say what evidence would change your mind.
- Disagree with a senior respectfully and clearly when you must: *'I see it differently, and here's why.'*

Admitting 'I don't know, I'll find out by Thursday' increases credibility when followed through.

steps.title: Fairness note
steps.body: Research and lived experience show 'presence' judgements can be biased against women, people with non-native accents, introverts and people from under-represented groups. As a leader, judge presence by substance and outcomes, sponsor people whose style differs from yours, and give specific, behavioural feedback rather than vague 'lacks presence' comments.

courses.title: Decisions under ambiguity and crisis leadership
courses.summary: Decide well when information is incomplete, lead calmly through outages, PR crises and layoffs, communicate during change, and sustain yourself as a leader.
outcomes: Learners can classify decisions by reversibility and speed
Learners can use pre-mortems and decision journals to reduce bias

scenes.text: VP Harish must decide whether to launch a new feature before the festive sale. His team keeps asking for 'one more week of data'.
Four weeks pass. A competitor launches first.
His mentor asks: 'Is this a one-way door or a two-way door? Could you launch to 5% of users and roll back?'
Next time, Harish launches to 5%, watches metrics for 48 hours, and scales up. Speed and safety together.

steps.title: One-way vs two-way doors
steps.body:
Jeff Bezos's shareholder letters popularised the distinction:
- **Two-way doors:** reversible decisions (feature flags, pricing tests, pilot launches). Decide **fast**, at lower levels, with ~70% of the information you'd like.
- **One-way doors:** hard or impossible to reverse (large acquisitions, exiting a market, major layoffs, architecture choices that lock you in). Decide **carefully**, with more analysis and senior involvement.

Many organisations treat every decision like a one-way door — and become slow.

steps.title: Tools for ambiguity
steps.body:
- **Pre-mortem** (Gary Klein): *'Imagine it's a year later and this failed. Why?'* Surfaces risks people hesitate to voice.
- **Decision journal:** write the decision, options, expected outcome, confidence, and what would change your mind. Review later to learn — judge decisions by the quality of the process, not only the outcome.
- **Disagree and commit:** after a fair debate, everyone commits fully even if they disagreed.
- **Decision rights** (e.g., RAPID: Recommend, Agree, Perform, Input, Decide) — clarify who decides.

steps.title: Worked example: a pre-mortem
Biases that distort decisions
steps.body:
- **Confirmation bias:** seeking data that supports what you already believe.
- **Sunk-cost fallacy:** continuing because you've already invested.
- **Anchoring:** first number dominates.
- **Overconfidence.**
- **Groupthink:** especially strong when juniors defer to seniors. Ask the most junior person to speak first.

lessons.title: Leading through an incident or crisis

story.title: UPI payments down on salary day

scenes.text: On the 1st of the month, a fintech's payment service fails. Thousands of merchants can't receive money. Social media erupts.
Ten senior people join the call; everyone gives instructions. Engineers don't know whom to listen to.
The Director of Engineering, Shreya, takes control: names an incident commander, a communications lead and a technical lead, and sets 30-minute updates.
Service is restored in 2 hours. The post-incident review is blameless and leads to three systemic fixes.

steps.title: Clear roles first
steps.body:
Many tech companies use an **incident command** model (inspired by emergency services):
- **Incident commander:** coordinates, decides priorities, doesn't debug.
- **Technical lead(s):** investigate and fix.
- **Communications lead:** updates stakeholders, customers and executives on a set cadence.
- **Scribe:** keeps a timeline.

Senior leaders should *support* the commander, not take over the call or demand constant updates from engineers.

steps.title: Crisis communication
steps.body:
- **Speak early**, even if you don't have all the answers: *'We're aware payments are failing for some merchants. We're working on it; next update by 3:30 pm.'*
- **Be honest** about what you know and don't know.
- **Regular cadence** (e.g., every 30 minutes) — silence breeds rumours.
- **Empathy** for affected customers.
- **Coordinate** with legal, PR and, where required, regulators — some sectors have mandatory incident-reporting obligations (for example, cyber incidents in India must be reported to CERT-In within prescribed timelines). Check with your legal and compliance teams.

steps.title: Worked example: status update template
steps.body:
*'[3:30 pm IST] Status: Investigating → Mitigating.*
*Impact: ~18% of merchant payments failing since 1:05 pm.*
*Cause (preliminary): database failover did not complete.*
*Actions: traffic shifted to secondary region; failure rate falling.*
*Next update: 4:00 pm.'*

steps.title: After the crisis
steps.body:
- **Blameless post-incident review** within days: timeline, contributing factors, what went well, action items with owners.
- **Thank people** publicly, especially those who worked overnight; give recovery time.
- **Follow through** on fixes — the credibility of the process depends on it.
- **Practise:** run game days or crisis simulations so roles are familiar before the real thing.

scenes.text: A news site reports that a Bengaluru tech company will cut 10% of staff. Leadership says nothing for a week while finalising details.
Productivity collapses. Top performers start interviewing elsewhere.
When the CEO finally speaks, she is honest: why, who is affected, how they'll be supported, and what happens next.
Survivors say the honesty mattered — but the week of silence cost the company good people.

steps.title: Why change communication fails
steps.body:
- **Silence** while 'details are finalised' fuels rumours.
- **Spin** ('right-sizing for exciting growth') destroys credibility.
- **One-time announcements** — people need to hear key messages several times.
- **Ignoring emotions** — fear, grief and anger are normal reactions to change.

steps.title: A structure for change messages
steps.body:
- **What's changing** (clearly, early).
- **Why** (the honest reason).
- **What it means for you** (the question everyone actually has).
- **What stays the same.**
- **What we don't know yet** and when we'll know.
- **Support available** (severance, outplacement, EAP, references).
- **Where to ask questions** (live Q&A, managers, FAQ).

Equip managers *before* the announcement with talking points and FAQs; they get most of the questions.

steps.title: Worked example: an honest opening
steps.body: *'Today I have hard news. We are reducing our team by about 10% — roughly 120 colleagues. This is because our growth has slowed and our costs are higher than we can sustain. It is not a reflection of the individuals affected. If you're affected, your manager and HR will speak with you today, and you'll receive [support details]. I'll host an open Q&A at 4 pm. I'm sorry; this is a decision leadership owns.'*

steps.title: Leading the survivors
steps.body: After layoffs, those who stay often feel guilt, fear and overload ('survivor syndrome'). Reset priorities explicitly (what we'll stop doing), hold team conversations, be visible and accessible, and avoid celebrating 'efficiency' right after people lost jobs.

lessons.title: Leading yourself: energy, judgement and support

story.title: The director who never switched off

scenes.text: Sanjay, a Senior Director, answers messages at 1 am, works weekends and takes pride in 'always being available'.
His decisions get worse; he snaps at managers in reviews. His team copies his hours and two managers burn out.
After a health scare, his doctor tells him to change.
He sets boundaries, delegates more, and visibly takes leave. Team performance improves — and so does his judgement.

steps.title: Your energy is an organisational resource
steps.body: Senior leaders set the norms. If you message at midnight, people assume they must reply. Sleep deprivation and chronic stress impair judgement, emotional regulation and memory. Protecting your energy is part of the job, not a luxury.

steps.title: Practical habits
steps.body:
- **Schedule-send** messages for working hours.
- Block **thinking time** each week for strategy.
- Take **real leave** and make it visible; delegate authority while away.
- Have a **personal board of advisers**: a mentor, a peer outside the company, a coach.
- Regular exercise, sleep and time with family or friends are performance tools.
- Review your decision journal monthly.

steps.title: Values under pressure
steps.body: Crises test values: pressure to hide bad news, cut corners on safety or compliance, or treat people unfairly. Decide your red lines *before* pressure hits. A useful test: *'Would I be comfortable if this decision and my reasoning were published on the front page — and explained to my own children?'*

steps.title: When to get help
steps.body: Persistent exhaustion, cynicism, sleep problems, irritability or low mood are warning signs. Leaders are not exempt. Talk to a doctor or counsellor; use your company's EAP; in India, Tele-MANAS (14416) offers free mental-health support. In an emergency, call 112.

corporate-communication.title: Communication that moves work
corporate-communication.description: Business writing, presenting, storytelling with data and cross-cultural communication for Indian and global teams — from a fresher's first email to a director's board memo.

courses.title: Business writing: clear, short, persuasive
courses.summary: Write like a strong professional: plain language, the pyramid principle, one-pagers and narrative memos for executives, and a repeatable editing process.
outcomes: Learners can rewrite wordy text into plain, active language
Learners can structure documents top-down with the pyramid principle and SCQA
Learners can write one-pagers and decision memos for executives
Learners can edit their own writing systematically

scenes.text: Rajiv, a project manager in Bengaluru, writes: 'It is hereby requested that, in view of the aforementioned considerations, necessary action may kindly be initiated at the earliest so as to facilitate the timely completion…'
His US client replies: 'Sorry, what do you need from us?'
His coach rewrites it: 'Please approve the test plan by Friday so we can finish on time.'
Thirteen words instead of ninety. Approved the same day.

steps.title: The plain-language rules
steps.body:
- **Short words:** *use* not *utilise*; *start* not *commence*; *help* not *facilitate*.
- **Short sentences:** aim for an average under ~20 words; one idea per sentence.
- **Active voice:** *'The team fixed the bug'* not *'The bug was fixed by the team'*. Active voice shows who does what.
- **Concrete over abstract:** *'Reduce delivery time from 5 to 3 days'* not *'optimise delivery efficiency'*.
- **Cut filler:** *'at this point in time'* → *now*; *'in order to'* → *to*; *'due to the fact that'* → *because*.

steps.title: Worked example: three rewrites
steps.body:
- *'The meeting has been rescheduled by the management due to unavoidable circumstances.'* → **'Management moved the meeting to Thursday because the client can't attend Wednesday.'**
- *'We would like to inform you that your request is under process.'* → **'We're working on your request and will reply by 5 pm tomorrow.'**
- *'Kindly revert with the needful at the earliest.'* → **'Please send the signed form by Monday.'**

Notice how each rewrite adds a **specific** fact (day, time, reason) — plain language is usually more informative, not less.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using jargon and acronyms for readers outside your team (spell out on first use: *'user acceptance testing (UAT)'*).
- Thinking formal = professional. Clarity is professional.
- Hedging everything: *'It might perhaps be possible that…'* — say what you think and how confident you are.
- Burying numbers in paragraphs; put key numbers where the eye lands.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Take your last long email. Cut it by 40% without losing any fact. Then read it aloud — if you run out of breath in a sentence, split it.

The client CFO interrupts on slide 4: 'What are you recommending?'
Her manager teaches her the pyramid: answer first, then 3 supporting reasons, then the evidence.
Her next deck opens with 'Close two of the five warehouses to save ₹18 crore a year' — and the CFO engages for an hour.

steps.title: Answer first, then support
steps.body:
The **pyramid principle** (popularised by Barbara Minto) says: start with your **main point**, then group supporting arguments (ideally three), each backed by evidence.

- **Top:** governing thought — *'We should close two of five warehouses.'*
- **Middle:** key reasons — *cost, service levels, risk.*
- **Bottom:** data — *rent, utilisation, delivery times.*

Busy readers can stop at any level and still get the message.

steps.title: SCQA for introductions
steps.body:
To set up the main point, use **Situation – Complication – Question – Answer**:
- **S:** *We run five warehouses in western India.*
- **C:** *Utilisation has dropped to 55% since we moved to direct-to-store shipping.*
- **Q:** *Should we keep all five?*
- **A:** *No — close Nashik and Rajkot and save about ₹18 crore a year with no loss of 2-day delivery.*

SCQA works for emails, memos, presentations and even interview answers.

steps.title: Worked example: a pyramid email
steps.body:
*Subject: Recommendation: move to vendor B for cloud backup (saves ₹14 lakh/yr)*

*Recommendation: switch to vendor B from 1 April.*
*Why:*
- *Cost: ₹14 lakh/year lower for the same storage.*
- *Reliability: 2 outages last year vs 7 for vendor A.*
- *Compliance: data stays in Indian data centres.*
*Risk: migration takes 3 weeks; we'll run both in parallel during that time.*
*Decision needed by 15 Feb.*

steps.title: MECE grouping
steps.body: Group supporting points so they are **MECE — mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive**: no overlaps, no big gaps. *'Cost, reliability, compliance'* is MECE-ish; *'cost, price, money'* overlaps. MECE thinking makes your argument feel complete and easy to follow.

activity.prompt: Arrange this SCQA introduction in order.
items: Situation: Our app has 2 million monthly users in India.
Complication: 40% drop off at the payment step.
Question: How do we reduce payment drop-off?
Answer: Add UPI autopay and one-tap retry — expected to recover a third of drop-offs.

quiz.q: In the pyramid principle, what comes first?
SCQA stands for…
quiz.why: A storytelling setup for your main point.

quiz.q: MECE means…
Why did the CFO interrupt Ishita?
options: The recommendation was buried at the end

lessons.title: One-pagers and decision memos for executives

story.title: The VP who reads at 7 am

scenes.text: Kabir needs his VP, Susan in Seattle, to approve hiring three engineers for a Bengaluru team. He has 10 minutes in her packed calendar.
Instead of 20 slides, he writes a one-page memo and sends it the evening before.
Susan reads it with her morning coffee, writes two questions in the margin, and the meeting takes six minutes.
Approved. 'This is how I like to decide,' she says.

steps.title: The one-page decision memo
steps.body:
A reliable structure:
- **Title + ask:** *'Decision: approve 3 backend hires for Payments (Q3)'*
- **Context (2–3 lines):** why now.
- **Recommendation:** what you propose.
- **Options considered:** 2–3 alternatives with pros/cons (including 'do nothing').
- **Impact:** cost, benefit, metrics.
- **Risks & mitigations.**
- **What we need from you:** the decision, by when.

Some companies, famously Amazon, use longer **narrative memos** read silently at the start of meetings instead of slides; the principle is the same: complete sentences force complete thinking.

steps.title: Worked example: options table
steps.body:
| Option | Cost/yr | Impact | Risk |
- **A. Hire 3 engineers (recommended):** ~₹1.2 crore; launch UPI autopay in Q4; hiring takes 8–10 weeks.
- **B. Use a vendor team:** ~₹1.5 crore; faster start; less ownership, knowledge leaves with vendor.
- **C. Do nothing:** ₹0; autopay slips to next year; competitors may win users.

Showing that you considered alternatives builds trust in your recommendation.

steps.title: Write for the executive's questions
steps.body: Executives tend to ask: *What do you need from me? Why now? What does it cost? What's the risk? What are the alternatives? How will we know it worked?* Answer all six on the page and your meeting will be short.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Hiding the ask on page 3.
- Only one option (looks like you didn't think).
- No numbers, or numbers without sources.
- Sending it five minutes before the meeting. Send it early enough to be read.

activity.prompt: Does your executive memo pass the checklist?
items: The ask and deadline are in the title or first line
Context is 2–3 lines
There's a clear recommendation
At least two alternatives, including 'do nothing'
Costs and benefits have numbers and sources
Risks and mitigations are listed
Success metrics are defined
It fits on one page
Sent early enough to be read

quiz.q: What should the first line of a decision memo contain?
quiz.why: Readers need to know what's being asked.

quiz.q: Why include 'do nothing' as an option?
options: It clarifies the cost of inaction

quiz.q: Narrative memos force…
quiz.why: Bullet fragments can hide gaps in logic.

quiz.q: Which question do executives commonly ask?
options: What's the risk and what are the alternatives?
quiz.why: Risk and options are core to decisions.

scenes.text: Leena, a policy analyst in Delhi, writes fast but her drafts are full of repetition and typos.
A senior editor teaches her a three-pass method: structure, sentences, then proofing.
It adds 15 minutes to each document.
Within a month, her director starts forwarding her drafts unchanged.

steps.title: Pass 1: structure
steps.body: Ask: Is the main point at the top? Does each section support it? Is anything missing or repeated? Would headings or bullets help? **Fix structure before polishing words** — no point perfecting a paragraph you'll delete.

steps.title: Pass 2: sentences
steps.body:
- Cut filler and repeated ideas.
- Change passive to active where it helps.
- Replace vague words (*'significant', 'various', 'some'*) with numbers or specifics.
- Check each paragraph starts with its point (a **topic sentence**).

steps.title: Pass 3: proofing
steps.body:
- Names, titles, dates, numbers, currency (₹ vs $), time zones.
- Spelling and grammar (spell-checkers help, but don't catch wrong-but-real words like *'form/from'*).
- Read aloud or use a read-aloud tool.
- Check attachments and links.

Grammar tools and AI assistants can help with drafts, but **never paste confidential company or client information into tools your company hasn't approved**, and always check AI output for errors.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Take a 300-word document you wrote. Do the three passes separately, with a short break between. Note how many words you cut and how many errors you caught.

statements.s: You should polish sentences before fixing the structure.
statements.why: Structure first; otherwise you polish text you'll cut.

statements.s: Spell-checkers catch every wrong word.
statements.why: They miss real words used wrongly, like 'form' for 'from'.

statements.s: Reading aloud helps catch awkward sentences and errors.
statements.why: Your ear catches what your eye skips.

statements.s: It's fine to paste confidential client data into any free AI tool to improve grammar.
statements.why: Use only company-approved tools for confidential data.

statements.s: Replacing 'significant increase' with 'a 23% increase' improves clarity.
statements.why: Specific numbers beat vague adjectives.

A topic sentence…
options: Ends a paragraph with a joke
States the paragraph's main point at the start

quiz.q: Which detail is most often wrong in business documents and worth checking?
Using AI writing tools at work requires…
options: Company-approved tools for confidential data and checking output

questions.q: 'Utilise' is better written as…
The pyramid principle starts with…
Active voice example:
options: The bug has been fixed by someone.

questions.q: SCQA's 'C' is…
A decision memo should include at least…
options: Two or more options including 'do nothing'

questions.q: MECE grouping avoids…
Which edit pass comes first?
Replace 'due to the fact that' with…
Why send a memo before the meeting?
options: So it can be read and the meeting used to decide

questions.q: Which group of reasons is closest to MECE?
An executive asks 'How will we know it worked?' You need…
Best rewrite of 'We would like to inform you that your request is under process'?
options: 'We're working on your request and will reply by 5 pm tomorrow.'

questions.q: A director says, 'Your memo is persuasive but I don't trust the numbers.' The most likely fix?
options: Add sources and assumptions for each number

courses.title: Presenting and storytelling with data
courses.summary: Structure talks, design clean slides, choose the right chart and tell a story with data, then handle Q&A and nerves with confidence.
outcomes: Learners can structure a presentation around one key message
Learners can design simple, readable slides with action titles
Learners can choose an honest, appropriate chart for data
Learners can handle Q&A and manage presentation anxiety

lessons.title: Structuring a talk around one message

scenes.text: Neel has 10 minutes at the quarterly town hall of his Pune company to present his team's work. He prepares 30 slides covering everything.
At minute 10 he's on slide 12. The host cuts him off.
A mentor asks him: 'If the audience remembers one sentence, what should it be?'
His next talk: one message, three supports, one ask. Seven slides. People quote his line afterwards.

steps.title: Start with the one-sentence message
steps.body:
Before opening PowerPoint, write: **'After this talk, the audience should ___ because ___.'** For example: *'…approve the pilot in Jaipur because it cut delivery time by 30% in Indore.'*

Everything that doesn't support that sentence is cut or moved to the appendix.

steps.title: A simple talk structure
steps.body:
- **Hook (30 sec):** a story, number or question. *'Last Diwali, 1 in 5 orders in Indore arrived late.'*
- **Message:** state it.
- **Three supports:** each a short section with evidence.
- **Ask / next step:** what you want the audience to do.
- **Close:** restate the message.

Rule of thumb: plan roughly **one to two minutes per content slide** and rehearse with a timer.

steps.title: Worked example: 'tell them' structure
steps.body:
Neel's revised outline:
- Hook: *'1 in 5 Diwali orders were late.'*
- Message: *'Micro-warehouses fixed it in Indore; let's do Jaipur next.'*
- Support 1: late deliveries fell from 20% to 6%.
- Support 2: cost per order fell by ₹11.
- Support 3: customer ratings rose from 3.9 to 4.4.
- Ask: approve ₹2 crore for the Jaipur pilot.
- Close: *'Fewer late Diwalis — Jaipur next.'*

steps.title: Know your audience
steps.body: Executives: decision, numbers, risk — fast. Engineers: how it works, trade-offs. Clients: their problem and outcome. Mixed audiences: lead with the outcome, offer detail in Q&A or an appendix.

activity.prompt: Complete the planning sentence and structure.
activity.text: After this talk, the audience should ___ because ___. Structure: hook, message, three supports, ___, close.
answers: it works|of the evidence|the results|the data

quiz.q: The first thing to prepare for a talk is…
A good hook is…
options: A striking story, number or question

quiz.q: What do you do with content that doesn't support your message?
options: Cut it or move it to an appendix

quiz.q: For executives you should emphasise…

scenes.text: Pallavi's slide has 14 bullet points in 11-point font. She reads them aloud while the audience reads ahead.
Half the room checks phones.
She redesigns: one point per slide, an action title, one chart, big font.
Now people look up at her when she speaks.

steps.title: Action titles
steps.body:
Replace topic titles with **action titles** — a full sentence that states the takeaway:
- Topic: *'Q3 sales'*
- Action: *'Q3 sales grew 18%, driven by Tier-2 cities'*

If someone reads only your titles, they should get the whole story.

steps.title: Clean design rules
steps.body:
- **One idea per slide.**
- Large, readable fonts (as a rough guide, body text around 24 pt or larger for projected slides).
- High contrast; avoid text on busy photos.
- Consistent colours: one highlight colour for 'the point'.
- Fewer words: slides support you; they're not your script.
- Make it **accessible**: don't rely on colour alone (some viewers are colour-blind); add labels.

steps.title: Worked example: before → after
steps.body:
**Before:** title *'Customer feedback'*, 12 bullets of comments.

**After:** title *'Customers love speed but hate our returns process'*; two big quotes; one bar chart showing 'returns' as the top complaint (38%) in your highlight colour, others in grey.

The audience understands in 5 seconds.

steps.title: Pre-read vs presented deck
steps.body: A deck to be **presented** should be sparse. A deck to be **read** (sent by email) needs more text. Don't use one for the other — or make a sparse main deck plus a detailed appendix.

activity.prompt: Topic title or action title?

items.text: Q3 revenue
Q3 revenue grew 18% on Tier-2 demand
Customer feedback
Returns are our #1 complaint (38%)
Next steps
Approve ₹2 crore to pilot Jaipur in Q1

quiz.q: An action title…
options: States the takeaway as a sentence

quiz.q: Why avoid relying only on colour?
A presented deck should be…
A highlight colour helps…
options: Draw attention to the key point

scenes.text: In a review, Arvind shows a bar chart where complaints 'tripled' — the bars look enormous.
The CFO notices the y-axis starts at 950. Complaints went from 980 to 1,010 — a 3% rise.
Arvind's credibility takes a hit. He hadn't meant to mislead; the tool set the axis automatically.
He now checks every chart: right type, honest axis, clear label.

steps.title: Pick the chart for the question
steps.body:
- **Compare categories:** bar chart (horizontal bars for long labels).
- **Change over time:** line chart.
- **Part of a whole:** stacked bar, or a pie only if there are few slices (around 2–4) with clearly different sizes.
- **Relationship between two numbers:** scatter plot.
- **Distribution:** histogram or box plot.
- **A single key number:** just show the number big, with context (*'₹4.2 crore, up 12% vs last year'*).

steps.title: Honesty rules
steps.body:
- **Bar charts must start at zero** — bar length represents the value. (Line charts may use a non-zero axis if clearly labelled.)
- Don't use 3D effects; they distort sizes.
- Label units and sources.
- Don't cherry-pick date ranges to hide bad periods.
- Show percentages *and* base numbers when the base is small (*'50% growth — from 4 to 6 customers'*).

steps.title: Worked example: the right comparison
steps.body:
Question: *'Which region has the highest return rate?'*
- Data: North 4.1%, South 2.9%, East 6.3%, West 3.5%.
- Best chart: **horizontal bar, sorted from highest to lowest**, East highlighted, others grey, action title *'East's return rate (6.3%) is double the South's'*.

Sorting is a small step that makes patterns obvious.

steps.title: Narrate the chart
steps.body: When presenting a chart: say **what it shows** (*'This is monthly churn'*), **where to look** (*'Focus on the red line after June'*), and **what it means** (*'Churn doubled after the price change'*). Audiences need a guide.

activity.prompt: Match the question to the best chart.
pairs: How did monthly sales change over two years?
Is ad spend related to sales across 50 cities?
A big single number with context

quiz.q: Why must bar charts start at zero?
options: Bar length represents value; truncating exaggerates differences

quiz.q: Best chart for change over time?
When is a pie chart acceptable?
options: With a few slices of clearly different sizes
quiz.why: Pies are hard to compare with many slices.

quiz.q: '50% growth' on a tiny base should be shown with…
Sorting bars from highest to lowest…

scenes.text: Ayesha presents to her company's leadership in Dubai. A director asks a question she can't answer. Her mind goes blank.
She remembers her coach: 'Pause. Repeat the question. If you don't know, say so and commit to follow up.'
'Good question — I don't have the Q2 split with me. I'll send it by 5 pm today.'
She sends it at 3 pm. The director later says her follow-through impressed him more than the presentation.

steps.title: Handling questions
steps.body:
- **Listen fully**; don't interrupt.
- **Pause** a second — it looks thoughtful.
- **Repeat or rephrase** the question (helps the room and buys time).
- **Answer briefly**, then check: *'Does that answer it?'*
- **Don't know?** *'I don't have that number; I'll send it by 5 pm.'* Then do it.
- **Hostile question?** Stay calm, acknowledge the concern, answer the fact: *'I understand the worry about cost. Here's the breakdown…'*

steps.title: Managing nerves
steps.body:
Nervousness is normal — even experienced speakers feel it. Practical tools:
- **Rehearse aloud** 2–3 times, at least once standing, with a timer.
- Know your **first 30 seconds** by heart.
- **Slow breathing** before you start (e.g., inhale 4, hold 4, exhale 4–6).
- Reframe: the audience wants you to succeed.
- Find 2–3 friendly faces and speak to them.

If anxiety is severe or stops you from working, a counsellor or psychologist can help — it's very treatable.

steps.title: Presence basics
steps.body:
- Stand or sit tall; plant your feet.
- Make eye contact (on video: look at the camera when making key points).
- Speak slower than feels natural; pause after key numbers.
- Cut fillers ('um', 'basically', 'actually') — a pause is better.
- On video, good lighting from the front and a clear microphone matter more than a fancy background.

steps.title: Try this
steps.body: Record yourself giving a 2-minute version of a talk on your phone. Watch it once for content, once for voice (pace, fillers) and once with the sound off (body language).

activity.label: Calm-before-you-present breath: in 4, hold 4, out 6, rest 2

quiz.q: You don't know the answer to a question. Best response?
options: Say you don't have it and commit to a specific follow-up time

quiz.q: Why repeat a question before answering?
options: It helps the room hear it and gives you thinking time

quiz.q: A good way to reduce nerves is…
options: Rehearse aloud and know your first 30 seconds

quiz.q: On a video call, for key points look at…

questions.q: Before building slides, write…
Best chart for trend over time?
An action title example is…
Bar charts should start at…
A hook is used to…
Unknown answer in Q&A?
options: Commit to follow up by a specific time

questions.q: Which is a misleading practice?
A deck emailed as a pre-read should be…
options: Identical to a sparse presented deck

questions.q: Relationship between ad spend and sales across cities is best shown with…
Complaints rose from 980 to 1,010 but the chart looks tripled. Likely cause?
options: Truncated y-axis on a bar chart

questions.q: Handling a hostile question well means…
options: Acknowledging the concern and answering with facts

questions.q: A mixed audience of engineers and executives: best approach?
options: Lead with outcome; keep technical detail for appendix/Q&A

questions.q: When narrating a chart, say…
options: What it shows, where to look, what it means

courses.title: Cross-cultural communication for global teams
courses.summary: Work smoothly with colleagues and clients in the US, Europe, Japan, the Middle East and across India: context, directness, feedback, time zones and Indian-English pitfalls.
outcomes: Learners can explain high- vs low-context communication
Learners can adapt directness and feedback style to a culture
Learners can avoid common Indian-English misunderstandings
Learners can run effective meetings across time zones and cultures

scenes.text: Mark, a manager in Chicago, asks his Indian team lead, Srinivas, 'Can we deliver by Friday?' Srinivas says, 'We will try our best.'
Mark hears 'yes'. Srinivas meant 'very unlikely, but I don't want to refuse you directly'.
Friday comes; nothing is delivered. Both feel let down.
After a cross-cultural workshop, Srinivas learns to say: 'Friday is not realistic; Tuesday is. Here's why.' Mark learns to ask, 'How confident are you, 1 to 10?'

steps.title: Two ends of a spectrum
steps.body:
Anthropologist Edward T. Hall described **high-context** and **low-context** communication:
- **Low-context** (often associated with the US, Netherlands, Germany, Scandinavia, Australia): meaning is in the explicit words. 'Yes' means yes. Directness is valued.
- **High-context** (often associated with Japan, China, Korea, much of India, the Middle East): meaning is also in tone, relationship, what is *not* said. Refusals may be indirect to preserve harmony.

These are **tendencies, not rules** — individuals vary a lot, and many Indians in global firms are quite direct.

steps.title: Worked example: translating 'we'll try'
steps.body:
Phrases that can mean 'probably not' in high-context speech:
- *'We will try our best.'* · *'It will be difficult.'* · *'Let me check and revert.'* · *'Should be possible, sir.'*

For low-context colleagues, be explicit: *'Friday isn't realistic because testing needs 3 days. We can deliver Tuesday, or deliver a partial version Friday without the reports module. Which do you prefer?'*

steps.title: Confidence scales
steps.body: A simple tool that works across cultures: state or ask for **confidence levels**. *'I'm 60% confident on Friday, 95% on Tuesday.'* It replaces vague 'we'll try' with something everyone can plan around, without anyone having to say a blunt 'no'.

steps.title: Reading the room elsewhere
steps.body: With Japanese colleagues, silence may mean thinking, not agreement; decisions may be built through informal consultation before meetings. With many Middle Eastern partners, relationship-building and hospitality come before business. With German or Dutch colleagues, blunt critique of an idea is often not personal. Ask colleagues from that culture what's normal — people appreciate the effort.

activity.prompt: Which phrasing is clear for a low-context reader?

items.text: We will try our best.
Friday isn't realistic; Tuesday is, because testing needs 3 days.
Let me check and revert.
I'm 60% confident on Friday and 95% on Tuesday.
It should be possible, sir.
I'll confirm by 4 pm IST whether Friday works.

quiz.q: In low-context communication, meaning is mainly in…
'We will try our best' may be heard by a US manager as…
Confidence levels help because…
options: They replace vague promises with plannable information

quiz.q: Cultural dimensions are…

lessons.title: Indian English that confuses global colleagues

scenes.text: Pradeep writes to his UK client: 'I have a doubt about the requirement.' The client worries he doubts the project.
He adds, 'Let's prepone the meeting.' The client searches for 'prepone'.
In a friendly call, the client asks about these phrases. They laugh and Pradeep learns which words travel.
He keeps his Indian English at home and with Indian teams — and switches to global English with clients.

steps.title: Indian English is a real variety
steps.body: Indian English is a legitimate variety of English with its own vocabulary — just like British, American or Australian English. Words like *prepone* are understood in India. The issue is only **mutual understanding**: some words confuse readers elsewhere.

steps.title: Common phrases and global alternatives
steps.body:
- *'I have a doubt'* → **'I have a question'** (elsewhere 'doubt' suggests distrust).
- *'Prepone'* → **'bring forward / move earlier'**.
- *'Revert'* → **'reply / get back to you'**.
- *'Do the needful'* → state the specific action.
- *'Out of station'* → **'travelling / away'**.
- *'Passed out of college in 2022'* → **'graduated in 2022'** (elsewhere 'passed out' means fainted!).
- *'Kindly adjust'* → explain what you're asking them to accept.
- *'Same to same'* → **'identical'**.

steps.title: Dates, numbers and time zones
steps.body:
- **Lakh and crore** are not understood globally: ₹1 lakh = 100,000; ₹1 crore = 10 million. For global readers write *'₹10 million (₹1 crore)'* or convert to USD with a date.
- Dates: 04/05 means 4 May in India and the UK but April 5 in the US. Write **'4 May 2026'**.
- Always add time zones: *'3 pm IST / 10:30 am BST'* (IST is UTC+5:30).

steps.title: Don't over-correct
steps.body: You don't need to hide your accent or identity. Clarity is the goal, not imitation. Global colleagues should also learn some context about India — good teams adapt both ways.

activity.prompt: Match the Indian-English phrase to a globally clear version.

quiz.q: For a UK client, 'I have a doubt' may sound like…
₹1 crore equals…
The clearest date format for global teams is…
IST is…

scenes.text: Sanne from Amsterdam reviews Rohit's design: 'This is not good. The flow is confusing. Redo section 2.'
Rohit, used to gentler feedback, feels crushed and thinks Sanne dislikes him.
Over a call, Sanne is warm and says she really likes his work. She just gives feedback directly.
Meanwhile Rohit's feedback to her ('maybe we could consider looking at…') was so soft she ignored it. They agree on a shared style.

steps.title: Direct vs indirect negative feedback
steps.body:
Researcher Erin Meyer (*The Culture Map*) notes that cultures differ in how directly they give negative feedback — and this doesn't always match how direct they are in general. Some cultures use **upgraders** ('absolutely wrong', 'totally inappropriate'); others use **downgraders** ('a bit', 'maybe', 'kind of').

When working across cultures, recalibrate: a 'maybe consider' from a Japanese colleague may be serious; a blunt line from a Dutch colleague may be routine.

steps.title: Worked example: one message, two styles
steps.body:
**For a direct-feedback culture:** *'Section 2 doesn't work: users can't find the pay button. Please move it above the fold.'*

**For an indirect-feedback culture:** *'Overall the design is strong. One area we might improve is section 2 — in testing, users struggled to find the pay button. What if it were higher on the page?'*

**Universal safe middle:** be specific about the problem, kind about the person, clear about the request.

steps.title: Agree on norms explicitly
steps.body: In global teams, discuss in a kick-off: *'How do we like to give feedback? How do we disagree in meetings? What does silence mean?'* Writing down a team charter saves months of misunderstanding.

steps.title: Disagreeing in meetings
steps.body: Some cultures (e.g., France, Israel, Netherlands) often see open debate as healthy; others prefer to avoid open confrontation, especially with seniors. If you're from a less confrontational culture, practise phrases: *'Let me offer a different view…'*, *'I see it differently because…'*. If you're from a debate culture, invite quieter colleagues: *'Priya, what's your view?'* and use written input before meetings.

a.text: Your German manager says in front of the team, 'Your estimate is wrong. It's too optimistic.' You feel embarrassed. What do you do?

choices.label: Ask what's driving their view and share your assumptions
choices.feedback: Treat it as a debate about the estimate, not a personal attack.

choices.label: Stay silent and assume they dislike you
choices.feedback: Likely misreading a direct style.

b.text: They explain testing usually takes twice as long. You disagree on one part. How do you say it?

choices.label: 'I agree on testing; I see the API work differently because we're reusing an existing module.'
choices.feedback: Clear, specific disagreement — exactly what a direct culture expects.

choices.label: 'Maybe… perhaps… whatever you think.'
choices.feedback: Your valid point gets lost.

c.text: You avoid them for a week. What would help?

choices.label: Ask in a 1:1 how they prefer to give and receive feedback
choices.feedback: Making norms explicit clears the air.

e1.text: You agree on a revised estimate together. Your manager respects your clear reasoning.

e2.text: The estimate stays unrealistic. Practise stating disagreement directly with reasons.

quiz.q: 'Downgraders' in feedback are words like…
A blunt comment from a Dutch colleague is most likely…
The universal safe feedback style is…
options: Specific about the problem, kind about the person, clear about the request

quiz.q: A team charter on communication norms helps…

scenes.text: Deepa in Bengaluru joins an 11 pm IST call every day with San Francisco. She's exhausted; the US team never notices.
She proposes rotating slots and moving updates to written async summaries.
The team agrees: two live calls a week at alternating times, a shared doc for daily updates, and decisions posted in the channel.
Deepa sleeps again, and the US team says decisions are clearer.

steps.title: Find and protect the overlap
steps.body: India (UTC+5:30) overlaps easily with Europe's morning, while the US West Coast has very little overlap with Indian working hours. Map everyone's working hours, find the overlap, and **reserve it for things that truly need live discussion** — decisions, conflicts, brainstorming. Everything else can be **asynchronous** (written).

steps.title: Async-first habits
steps.body:
- Daily written updates in a shared doc or channel.
- Recorded demos instead of live ones.
- Decisions documented with context and owners.
- Clear 'reply-by' times with time zones (*'by 10 am PT / 10:30 pm IST'*).
- Handover notes at the end of each day ('follow-the-sun' teams).

steps.title: Share the pain fairly
steps.body: If late calls are unavoidable, **rotate** times so one region doesn't always sacrifice. Leaders should notice who is always on at midnight. Raising this is legitimate: *'Could we rotate the weekly sync? India has had the late slot for six months.'*

steps.title: Holidays and calendars
steps.body: Check holidays in all regions (Thanksgiving in the US, Golden Week in Japan, Ramadan schedules in the Gulf, Diwali/Pongal/Onam in India). Note that many Gulf countries have a Friday–Saturday or Saturday–Sunday weekend depending on the country — check rather than assume. Put a shared holiday calendar in your team space.
